1.summary: The Power-On Self-Test (POST) is a program stored on the motherboard ROM that runs every time the computer is booted; it instructs every hardware device on the motherboard to run its own built-in diagnostic and report the result back.
1.deeper:
When you press the ON button, the power supply turns on first, checks itself for correct output voltage, and sends a signal down the power good wire to wake up the CPU. When the CPU energizes, it immediately applies a built-in address to the address bus; this address is the first line of the POST program on the motherboard ROM. POST then has each hardware device test itself and report back. After POST is finished, in a BIOS environment it passes control to the BIOS program, also located on motherboard ROM, whose bootstrap loader goes on to find an operating system.

POST beep codes: if anything fails POST, the computer informs the user through audible beep codes from the motherboard speaker, or through numeric or text error codes on the display. Bad or missing video, for example, is often indicated by one long beep followed by two or three short beeps, and a single beep that repeats indefinitely indicates bad or missing RAM. Text error codes, such as CPU Fan Error, are usually self-explanatory.
1.analogy: POST is like a pilot's walk-around before a flight: every key part is checked before anything else happens, and a problem is called out before the trip starts.
1.scenario: An airman presses the ON button and hears one long beep followed by two short beeps instead of a normal start. POST has found a failure, and that pattern often means bad or missing video, so the airman knows the problem is often bad or missing video.
1.example: A smoke alarm tests itself when its button is pressed and chirps if something is wrong. POST has each device test itself at every start. In the course: POST instructs every hardware device on the motherboard to run its own built-in diagnostic and then report back the result to POST, Study Guide p.4.

1.summary: The bootstrap loader is a few lines of code in the BIOS whose job is to find an operating system, checking the storage devices in the boot order the CMOS settings give.
1.deeper: After POST is finished, the computer needs a way to find programs on a hard disk drive to start the operating system. In a BIOS environment, POST passes control to the BIOS program, which is also located on motherboard ROM. The bootstrap loader consists of a few lines of code in the BIOS, and its job is to find an operating system. It reads the CMOS instructions to determine the boot order: the CMOS settings are user-configurable and instruct the bootstrap loader where to look for an operating system and in which order of priority to check. For example, the settings may say to check a portable USB storage device first, then the internal optical drive, then the internal HDD; with several HDDs, their boot priority can be set as well. If the bootstrap loader locates a good boot sector, it passes control to the operating system and erases itself from memory.
1.analogy: The bootstrap loader is like a courier with a list of addresses in priority order: the courier tries each one in turn until the package is found, hands it over, and then leaves.
1.scenario: An airman wants a computer to start from a USB storage device. The airman sets the CMOS boot order to check the USB device first. At the next start-up, after POST passes control to the BIOS, the bootstrap loader reads that order and checks the USB device before the internal drives.
1.example: A person looking for keys checks the usual places in the same order every time: pocket, desk, then car. In the course: the bootstrap loader consists of a few lines of code in the BIOS whose job is to find an operating system, Study Guide p.4.

1.summary: The boot sector is a special, specific sector reserved on a storage device; its special programming tells the computer where the operating system is.
1.deeper: All storage devices (HDDs, solid-state drives, USB thumb drives, CDs and DVDs) can be configured to boot an operating system by reserving a special, specific sector called the boot sector. Bootable devices contain special programming on the boot sector that tells the computer the location of the operating system. A storage device with a usable operating system written on it is called a bootable disk or a system disk. During start-up, the bootstrap loader looks for a good boot sector in the order the CMOS settings give. If it locates a good boot sector, it passes control to the operating system and erases itself from memory. If it does not find one, it checks the next storage device specified in the CMOS settings. If it cannot find a good boot sector on any storage device, the monitor displays the error message "boot device not found" or "no bootable device".
1.analogy: A boot sector is like a sign at the door of each building that says which room the meeting is in. A visitor tries the buildings in a set order; at the first one with a good sign, the visitor follows it in. With no sign at any building, the visitor reports that no meeting was found.
1.scenario: An airman's computer is set in the CMOS to check a USB drive first, then the internal hard disk. The USB drive plugged in has no good boot sector, so the bootstrap loader moves on to the hard disk, finds a good boot sector there and passes control to the operating system.

1.summary: BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) is the built-in, non-volatile firmware on motherboard ROM that initializes the hardware at start-up and loads the operating system; it is now legacy technology.
1.deeper: BIOS is non-volatile firmware: lines of code permanently stored on motherboard ROM, typically in an EEPROM or flash memory, so it is always available and is not damaged by disk failures. It determines what a computer can do without accessing programs from a disk and contains the code to control the keyboard, display screen, disk drives and serial communications. Its most important task is to load the operating system: when the CPU tries to execute its first instruction, it cannot get it from the OS, which is on a hard disk, so the BIOS provides it. BIOS also runs the POST, activates other BIOS chips on installed cards, provides low-level routines the OS uses to interface with hardware devices, and manages settings for the hard disks and clock. BIOS is invisible to the user, although it may be updated by flashing the BIOS. CMOS, on the other hand, refers to the menu of hardware settings and options available to the user. BIOS is now considered legacy technology: UEFI replaced it, though many technicians still call both of them BIOS.
1.analogy: BIOS is like the first page of a manual sealed inside a machine: it is always there, it tells the machine how to wake its parts and where to find the rest of its instructions, and the owner never edits it. The CMOS menu is the settings panel beside it, which the owner can change.
1.scenario: An airman powers on a computer. Before any disk is read, the CPU needs its first instruction, and the BIOS on the motherboard ROM provides it: BIOS runs POST, initializes the hardware and loads the operating system. Later the airman opens the CMOS menu to change a setting; the BIOS code itself stays invisible to the user, although it may be updated by flashing.
1.example: A smoke detector has its program built in at the factory and works as soon as it gets power, without loading anything from outside. In the course: BIOS is lines of code permanently stored on a ROM chip on the motherboard, Study Guide p.15.

1.summary: The Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) is the replacement for BIOS: newer, more user friendly firmware that expands on BIOS in bootstrapping, network booting, disk partitioning, hardware security, user interface and cryptography.
1.deeper:
BIOS is non-volatile firmware, lines of code permanently stored on motherboard ROM, used to initialize motherboard hardware when the computer is first started; it is now considered legacy technology. UEFI was adopted by Intel, AMD, Microsoft and the PC industry in 2007 as a replacement for BIOS, and nearly every computer made since 2014 is UEFI compliant. It may be pronounced "yoo-fee" or shortened to "EFI" in print. UEFI also supports backward compatibility with legacy BIOS, and many technicians still lump the two together and call both of them BIOS.

The difference shows in the CMOS menu: a legacy BIOS menu is primitive-looking and often text-only, with choices made using the arrow keys and ENTER, while a UEFI menu offers a modern-looking graphical user interface (GUI) with mouse support. UEFI matters for disks too: the GUID Partition Table (GPT) is a subset of the UEFI specification, so it can only be used with modern motherboards that have UEFI enabled.
1.analogy: If BIOS is basic life support for the motherboard, UEFI is the full hospital ward: it still keeps the patient going, and it adds monitors, security and a far easier way for staff to work.
1.scenario: An airman opens the start-up settings on two computers. The older one shows a plain, text-only screen that the airman moves through with the arrow keys and ENTER. The newer one shows a graphical menu the airman can click with the mouse, and it can boot from the network and use a GPT disk: that one has UEFI.
1.example: A phone with a touch screen replaced the old keypad phone but can still make the same plain calls. UEFI replaced BIOS and still supports legacy BIOS. In the course: UEFI was adopted by Intel, AMD, Microsoft, and the PC industry in 2007 as a replacement for BIOS, Study Guide p.5.

1.summary: Random Access Memory (RAM), also called main memory or primary memory, is the volatile memory where the CPU works; it keeps data and programs only as long as power is applied.
1.deeper:
RAM is the best-known form of computer memory. It is "random access" because the CPU can access any memory cell directly. It is used for temporary storage of data and programs, and it is the space where the CPU works and performs much of its processing. Its speed and capacity increase with every generation, and the quantity and type of RAM installed is a major player in a computer's performance and the quality of the user experience. Two basic types are used in modern computers: Dynamic RAM (DRAM) and Static RAM (SRAM).

Do not confuse memory with storage. Long-term storage of operating systems, applications and user data uses a nonvolatile medium such as a hard disk drive, solid state drive or optical drive, called secondary memory or secondary storage. A computer uses RAM the way a math teacher uses a chalk board, while storage is like the teacher's file cabinet.
1.analogy: RAM is the math teacher's chalk board: the work happens there, and it is wiped when the class ends. Storage is the file cabinet, where the papers stay until someone takes them out.
1.scenario: An airman opens a large report, and the program and the report are loaded from the hard disk drive into RAM, where the CPU works on them. When the computer is shut down, RAM keeps nothing; the saved report stays on the drive.
1.example: A desk is where papers are spread out while you work; at the end of the day they go back into the cabinet. RAM is the computer's desk. In the course: RAM is volatile memory because it will retain data only as long as power is applied, Study Guide p.5.

1.summary: Dynamic RAM (DRAM) is the most common form of computer memory; its cells must be refreshed constantly, or they forget what they hold.
1.deeper:
Each DRAM memory cell pairs a transistor and a capacitor to hold one bit of data. The capacitor holds the bit, a 0 or a 1; the transistor acts as a switch that lets the control circuitry on the memory chip read the capacitor or change its state. A capacitor is like a small bucket that stores electrons: full for a 1, empty for a 0. The bucket leaks, and in a few milliseconds a full bucket becomes empty.

So either the CPU or the memory controller must recharge every capacitor holding a 1 before it discharges: the memory controller reads the memory and writes it right back. This refresh happens automatically thousands of times per second, and it is where Dynamic RAM gets its name. The downside is that refreshing takes time and slows down the memory. Static RAM (SRAM) never needs a refresh and is faster but more expensive, so DRAM, cheap and slow, forms the larger system memory.
1.analogy: A DRAM cell is a leaky bucket. To keep a full bucket full, someone must keep topping it up, over and over, many times a second. That constant topping up is the refresh, and the time it takes is why DRAM is slower.
1.scenario: An airman reads that the main memory of a computer is DRAM. The capacitor in each cell that holds a 1 starts to leak at once, so the memory controller keeps reading the memory and writing it right back, thousands of times per second, so no data is forgotten.
1.example: A chalk line on a playground fades unless someone keeps drawing it again. DRAM must be redrawn the same way, all the time. In the course: DRAM must be dynamically refreshed all the time, or it forgets what it is holding, Study Guide p.6.

1.summary: Static RAM (SRAM) holds each bit in a circuit called a flip-flop that never has to be refreshed, so it is significantly faster than Dynamic RAM (DRAM); it is also more expensive and is used in the CPU's speed-sensitive cache.
1.deeper: A flip-flop for an SRAM memory cell takes four to six transistors along with some wiring. Because it never has to be refreshed, SRAM holds its data as long as power is applied, but it is still volatile. DRAM, by contrast, pairs a transistor and a capacitor in each cell; the capacitor leaks, so the memory controller must refresh DRAM thousands of times per second, and that refreshing slows the memory down. Because a static cell has more parts, it takes up a lot more space on a chip, so SRAM gives less memory per chip and costs more. In short, SRAM is fast and expensive and DRAM is cheap and slow: SRAM is used in the CPU's speed-sensitive cache, typically a 3-level hierarchy named L1, L2 and L3, and DRAM forms the larger system memory.
1.analogy: SRAM is like a light switch: flipped on, it stays on with nothing more to do. DRAM is like a leaky bucket that someone must keep topping up, which takes time.

1.summary: Synchronous DRAM (SDRAM) chips use the common system clock signal, so they coordinate CPU and memory operations more efficiently; modern computer systems use them.
1.deeper: Asynchronous DRAM, such as the original Fast Page Mode (FPM) DRAM and Extended Data-out (EDO) DRAM, is not synchronized with the CPU clock. SDRAM chips are. Plain SDRAM takes advantage of burst mode to improve performance: it stays on the row that holds the requested bit and moves rapidly through the columns, reading each bit as it goes. Double Data Rate (DDR) SDRAM is just like SDRAM except that it has higher bandwidth, meaning greater speed. DDR2 SDRAM, the second version, almost doubles the speed of plain DDR SDRAM, and DDR3 SDRAM virtually doubles the access speed again. The various revisions of DDR SDRAM can be identified by sight from the location of the notch on the RAM stick. Memory comes on small circuit cards called sticks, in DIMM or SO-DIMM versions.
1.analogy: SDRAM is like a rowing crew that pulls to the beat of one drummer: because everyone keeps the same time, the work moves together without waiting.
1.scenario: An airman sorts a box of RAM sticks from older computers into DDR, DDR2 and DDR3 SDRAM. Without reading any labels, the airman tells the revisions apart by sight, from the location of the notch on each stick.
1.example: A marching band stays in step because every player follows the same drum beat. SDRAM chips follow the same system clock. In the course: Synchronous DRAM (SDRAM) chips use the common system clock signal and more efficiently coordinate the CPU and memory operations, Study Guide p.7.

1.summary: A major memory failure is an error that causes the system to lock up, typically producing a Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) or a General Protection Fault (GPF).
1.deeper:
A major memory failure is an error serious enough to lock up the system. It typically produces one of two error types, and both can produce a Blue Screen of Death (BSOD).

Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI): an interrupt the CPU cannot ignore.

General Protection Fault (GPF): a system condition that causes a Windows application to crash. Its most common cause is two applications trying to use the same block of memory, or more specifically, one application trying to use memory assigned to another application.
1.analogy: A major memory failure is like a traffic jam that stops the whole road. Sometimes a siren goes off that every driver must obey (the NMI); sometimes one car crashes because it tried to park in a space that belongs to another (the GPF). Either way, the road can end up closed (the BSOD).
1.scenario: An airman's Windows computer locks up. The error shows that one application tried to use memory assigned to another, a General Protection Fault, and the screen turns to a Blue Screen of Death.
1.example: Two people trying to sit in the same seat stop a whole row from settling down. Two applications using the same block of memory is the most common cause of a GPF. In the course: a major memory failure is an error that causes the system to lock up, Study Guide p.9.

1.summary: Clock speed is the fastest speed at which a CPU can operate; the CPU clock produces a regular, pulsed electrical signal that synchronizes every CPU operation.
1.deeper:
Clock speed is an important parameter of CPU performance: it is the fastest speed at which a CPU can operate. The CPU clock produces a regular, repetitive, pulsed electrical signal that synchronizes every CPU operation; the clock is the drummer that the CPU and the whole motherboard march to. Clock speeds have increased dramatically since the invention of the CPU: the Intel 8088 CPU, developed in 1979, had a clock speed of 4.77MHz, while modern high-performance CPUs can have a base clock speed greater than 5GHz. Many PC gaming enthusiasts deliberately overclock their CPU in pursuit of better performance.

Quartz oscillator: the clock signal originates from a special circuit on the main board called a quartz oscillator.
1.analogy: Clock speed is like the beat of a metronome for a band: every player moves on the beat, and the fastest beat the band can keep up with is its top tempo.
1.scenario: An airman reads the specifications of two CPUs. One, like the 1979 Intel 8088, lists a clock speed of 4.77MHz; the other, a modern high-performance CPU, lists a base clock speed greater than 5GHz. 1.summary: The chipset is the array of integrated circuits on the motherboard that enables the CPU to communicate with RAM and the input/output devices; it defines the type of CPU and RAM the motherboard requires and the built-in devices it supports.
1.deeper:
The two most prominent features of a motherboard are its form factor and its chipset. The chipset determines the built-in devices the board supports, including expansion slots, and those built-in components in turn determine the core functionality of the system. The many responsibilities of the chipset are divided into two main functions, called Northbridge and Southbridge. ROM is another important member of the chipset, and the USB host controller is built into it.

Northbridge chipset function: it provides a high-speed interface between the CPU and other high-speed motherboard devices, including RAM and the video graphics adapter. In older computers the Northbridge is a discrete chip separate from the CPU; in modern computers the Northbridge function is integrated into the CPU itself.

Southbridge chipset function: a second chip that serves as the interface between the CPU and low-speed devices, including the USB controller and the hard disk drive controller. In modern PCs it has also absorbed the keyboard controller function. It is called the Input/Output Controller Hub in Intel systems and the Fusion Controller Hub in AMD systems, and some newer systems call it the Platform Controller Hub.
1.analogy: The chipset works like a building's front desk with two counters: an express counter for the few visitors who need fast service and a general counter for everyone else. The CPU sends fast work to one and slower work to the other.
1.scenario: An airman traces how a computer's parts talk to the CPU. RAM and the video graphics adapter need a very fast connection, so they go through the Northbridge, which on a modern computer is inside the CPU itself. The USB controller and the hard disk drive controller are slower devices, so they go through the Southbridge.
1.example: A transit hub decides which trains can stop at a station and which lines connect there. The chipset decides which CPU, RAM and built-in devices a motherboard works with. In the course: chipset defines the type of CPU and RAM the motherboard requires and determines the built-in devices it supports, Study Guide p.10.

1.summary: Form factor refers to the physical dimensions of the motherboard: its shape, size and mounting characteristics. The case, power connections and power supply must match it.
1.deeper:
Form factor is one of the two most prominent features of a motherboard; the other is the chipset. The form factor affects the case layout, the positioning of components on the motherboard, and the power supply's positioning and connections. Because of it, motherboard, case and power supply manufacturers know their products will integrate and operate with other parts designed to the same form factor standard.

Desktop motherboards have been standardized to fit various case sizes, and most use ATX, MicroATX (µATX) or ITX. ATX (12 x 9.6 inches) replaced the obsolete AT and baby AT form factors; created by Intel in 1995, it rotated the board layout 90 degrees, putting the disk drive cable connectors closer to the drive bays and the CPU closer to the power supply and cooling fan, and it remains a popular choice for enterprise and home systems. ITX comes in three sizes: Mini (6.7 x 6.7 inches), Nano (4.7 x 4.7 inches) and Pico (3.8 x 2.8 inches). The largest, Mini-ITX, is by far the most popular for small form factor (SFF) desktop computers, and ITX boards offer lower power consumption and silent, fan-less operation.
1.analogy: A form factor is like a standard picture-frame size: a print made to the standard fits any frame made to the same standard, and the frame maker never needs to see the print first.
1.scenario: An airman builds a small desktop for a cramped office and wants low power use and quiet, fan-less operation. The airman picks a Mini-ITX motherboard and a case made for that form factor, because the case and power supply must match the board's form factor.
1.example: Shoes come in standard sizes, so a shoe made to a size fits a foot of that size and a box made for it. Motherboards follow standard form factors in the same way. 1.summary: Read Only Memory (ROM) is an important member of the chipset that stores small programs called services, the code needed to operate common motherboard hardware; it is nonvolatile, so its code is not erased when the computer is turned off.
1.deeper: The services stored on the ROM chip are lines of code necessary for the operation of common motherboard hardware, such as the keyboard controller. ROM differs from RAM in two important ways. First, ROM is nonvolatile and is considered permanent memory: the code stored on it is not erased when the computer is turned off. Second, ROM chips are read-only: once a program is stored on one, it cannot easily be changed. ROM is intended to be read from often and written to rarely, but it can be updated by a specific operation called flashing the ROM, or flashing the BIOS. Most modern ROM chips are made of flash memory, the same kind of memory used for thumb drives, SD cards and solid-state drives. The POST and BIOS programs are stored on the motherboard ROM.
1.analogy: ROM is like the instructions printed inside the lid of a machine: they are there every time you open it, they do not fade when the power is off, and changing them takes a special job, not a pencil.
1.scenario: The code on a motherboard's ROM needs an update. The airman cannot simply write to it the way a program writes to RAM; the airman updates it with the specific operation called flashing the ROM (flashing the BIOS). The new code then stays on the chip when the computer is off.
1.example: A printed reference card on a desk is read many times a day but reprinted only rarely. ROM is read often and written rarely in the same way. In the course: ROM is intended to be read from often and written to rarely, Study Guide p.13.

1.summary: The CMOS menu gives the user control over the PC hardware settings, such as password and security settings, boot device order, internal device options, and the system clock and calendar.
1.deeper: Every PC has a program built into the system ROM, called the CMOS setup program or system setup utility, that lets the user modify and save CMOS settings. CMOS refers to the menu of hardware settings and options available to the user, while BIOS is the code on the ROM chip that the user does not see. A legacy BIOS CMOS menu is very primitive-looking and often text-only, with choices selected using the arrow keys and the ENTER key; a modern UEFI CMOS menu offers a modern-looking GUI with mouse support. The CMOS settings are user-configurable and instruct the bootstrap loader where to look for an operating system and in which order of priority to check. The BIOS interface and CMOS settings may be protected with a password. In older computers, if the CMOS battery runs down or is removed, all the CMOS settings return to their factory default values; in many modern computers the user hardware settings are stored on nonvolatile flash memory, and the only purpose of the CMOS battery is to maintain the motherboard clock and calendar while the computer is off.
1.analogy: The CMOS menu is like the settings screen of a phone: the phone's built-in software stays hidden, but the settings screen lets the owner choose the lock code, the clock and other options.
1.scenario: An airman opens the CMOS menu of an older computer whose battery was removed and finds every setting back at its factory default value. The airman sets the password and security settings, the boot device order and the system clock and calendar again.

1.summary: The central processing unit (CPU) is the principal component, the "brain" of a computer: it carries out program instructions by performing basic arithmetic, logic, controlling and I/O operations.
1.deeper:
The CPU tells all the other components what to do and when to do it. Modern CPUs are highly sophisticated microprocessors: specialized integrated circuits that combine multiple functions onto a single chip. Though internal design varies by manufacturer and generation, there are generally three main structures inside a CPU: the control unit, the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) and a small amount of high-speed memory called registers. The control unit directs the operation of the processor and the flow of data between the CPU and other devices, and registers hold an instruction, a storage address or any kind of data. RAM, outside the CPU, is the space where the CPU works and performs much of its processing.

Arithmetic logic unit: the ALU is a digital electronic circuit located inside the CPU, designed to perform math operations on binary integers. It performs all the processes related to arithmetic and logic operations that need to be done on instructions, and it can be designed to calculate any operation.
1.analogy: A CPU is like a restaurant kitchen: the head chef (the control unit) says who does what and when, the cook at the stove (the ALU) does the actual work on each order, and the small counter right at hand (the registers) holds what is being worked on now. The pantry down the hall is RAM.
1.scenario: An instruction tells the computer to add the contents of two registers. Inside the CPU, the control unit directs the instruction, the two values sit in registers, and the ALU performs the math on the binary integers; the result is placed in a specified register.
1.example: A person's brain tells the hands what to do and when to do it. In the course: The CPU is the "brain" of the computer which tells all the other components what to do and when to do it, Study Guide p.17.

1.summary: A register is one of a small set of data holding places located inside the CPU, made of high-speed volatile memory that the CPU uses to rapidly perform internal operations.
1.deeper:
There are generally three main structures inside a CPU: the control unit, the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) and registers. A register may hold an instruction, a storage address or any kind of data, such as a bit sequence or individual characters. Some instructions name registers as part of the instruction: for example, an instruction may say that the contents of two defined registers be added together and placed in a specified register. A register must be large enough to hold an instruction: in a 64-bit computer, a register must be 64 bits in length; some designs also have smaller half-registers for shorter instructions. A CPU may contain several kinds of registers, numbered or given distinctive names.

Do not confuse registers with CPU cache. Cache is additional hardware memory, a 3-level hierarchy of SRAM named L1, L2 and L3, located inside the CPU or on a chip directly adjacent to it; it stores frequently accessed data to reduce the time and energy needed to fetch data from RAM.
1.analogy: Registers are like the few slots on a cashier's counter right under the cashier's hands: tiny, but whatever sits there can be used at once. Cache is more like the shelf just behind the counter.
1.scenario: An airman reads a CPU instruction that says to add the contents of two named registers and put the result in a third register. The CPU does this inside itself, using its registers as quick holding places.
1.example: A cook keeps the few ingredients for the dish in progress right on the cutting board, not in the pantry. Registers are the CPU's cutting board. In the course: a register is one of a small set of data holding places located inside the computer central processing unit, Study Guide p.19.

1.summary: CPU cache is additional hardware memory in or right next to the CPU that stores frequently accessed data, reducing the time and energy needed to fetch data from RAM.
1.deeper: Modern CPUs have additional hardware memory called cache, located inside the CPU itself or on a hardware chip directly adjacent to it, which greatly reduces latency. The CPU uses cache to store frequently accessed data, reducing the time and energy required to fetch the data from RAM. Cache is typically implemented as a 3-level hierarchy of static RAM (SRAM) named L1, L2 and L3. SRAM is much faster than the dynamic RAM (DRAM) used for main memory, but it is more expensive and gives less memory per chip: that is why SRAM is used in the CPU's speed-sensitive cache and DRAM forms the larger system memory. The overall purpose of CPU cache is to improve the performance of the computer by letting the CPU process tasks more quickly. Registers are different: a small set of data holding places inside the CPU, made of high-speed volatile memory, that the CPU uses to perform internal operations.
1.analogy: CPU cache is like keeping the tools you use most on your workbench instead of in the shed: the shed (RAM) still holds everything, but most of the time what you need is already within reach.
1.scenario: While a program runs, the CPU keeps asking for the same data. Instead of fetching it from RAM each time, the CPU keeps it in its L1, L2 and L3 cache, right next to it, so it spends less time and energy fetching and processes tasks more quickly.
1.example: A cook keeps salt and oil beside the stove instead of walking to the pantry for every pinch. In the course: The CPU uses cache to store frequently accessed data to reduce the amount of time and energy required to fetch the data from RAM, Study Guide p.19.

1.summary: Storage media, also known as secondary memory or secondary storage, is a recording device, such as a hard disk drive (HDD), for storing large amounts of information.
1.deeper:
Although both an HDD and RAM are memory, it is more appropriate to call RAM main memory or primary memory and an HDD secondary memory or secondary storage. Electronic data storage needs electrical power to store and retrieve data, but most storage media are permanent (non-volatile): the data remains stored when power is removed. Storage devices fall into three categories. Magnetic storage includes hard disk drives, floppy disk drives and tape drives. Solid-state storage includes flash drives, solid-state drives (SSD), thumb drives, jump drives and SD (secure digital) memory cards.

Optical storage includes CD-ROM, DVD and Blu-ray discs. These discs are read with a laser, from the pits and lands recorded on the disc.
1.analogy: Storage media are like a library's shelves, sorted into three sections by how the books are made. The reading desk where you work on one book at a time is main memory, not a shelf.
1.scenario: An airman sorts a box of old equipment by storage category: the hard disk drives and a tape drive go in the magnetic pile, the CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs in the optical pile, and the thumb drives, SD cards and an SSD in the solid-state pile. The RAM sticks go aside, since RAM is main memory, not storage media.
1.example: A home keeps photos in albums, in shoe boxes and on a phone: three kinds of keeping place for the same pictures. Storage media come in three categories in the same way. In the course: storage devices fall into three categories: magnetic storage, optical storage, and solid-state storage, Study Guide p.20.

1.summary: Advanced Technology Attachment (ATA) is the most common hard drive connection standard; it comes in two major categories, Parallel ATA (PATA) and Serial ATA (SATA).
1.deeper:
There are two major types of storage drives, platter-based and solid state, and ATA is the most common hard drive connection standard. Its two major categories are Parallel ATA (PATA) and Serial ATA (SATA).

Parallel ATA: PATA is the older standard. It uses 40 or 80 pin ribbon cables plus hardware jumpers for configuration. PATA is legacy, and an airman is unlikely to encounter it on the job.

Serial ATA: SATA uses a thin, flexible cable and transfers data much faster. It is the prevailing standard, and most SATA based drives do not require any hardware jumper configuration: just plug them in. External SATA (eSATA) is an extension of the SATA standard for external hard drives. A drive may instead use the Serial Attached SCSI (SAS) standard, popular on servers: a SATA drive is compatible with the SAS bus, but an SAS drive cannot interface with a SATA bus.
1.analogy: PATA and SATA are like an old wide ribbon of many wires next to a slim modern cable: both connect the same kind of drive, but the slim one needs no extra setting before use and moves data faster.
1.scenario: An airman replaces the hard drive of an older desktop and finds a wide 80 pin ribbon cable and a jumper on the drive: a PATA connection. In a newer desktop, the drive connects with a thin, flexible SATA cable and needs no jumper setting; the airman just plugs it in.
1.example: A slim modern charging cable and an older bulky one can both connect a device, but the slim one is easier to plug in and use. In the course: ATA (Advanced Technology Attachment) is the most common hard drive connection standard, Study Guide p.21.

1.summary: Partitioning is the process of dividing the physical hard drive into smaller units called partitions; it is the first step in preparing a hard disk drive (HDD) for use.
1.deeper:
A new drive is like an empty file cabinet with no dividers, folders or labels; to make it useful it must be conditioned, that is, partitioned and then formatted. Partitioning makes the hard drive visible to the operating system, so an HDD must have at least one partition in order to function. In Microsoft Windows each partition is assigned a drive letter: the familiar C: drive is simply the C: partition. After an HDD is partitioned, it must be formatted with a suitable file system, which allows the disk to store and retrieve data in an organized manner.

Two partitioning systems divide a disk. MBR is the legacy system: a maximum of four primary partitions, or three primary partitions and one extended partition, and Windows must be installed on a primary partition. GPT is the newer system used by modern computers, allowing a vast number of partitions; it is a subset of the UEFI specification. Windows includes a partitioning menu in its installation process, a command-line utility called DiskPart and a graphical utility called Disk Management.
1.analogy: Partitioning is like putting dividers into an empty file cabinet so each section can get its own label. Formatting then adds the folders that let you store and find things in order.
1.scenario: An airman installs a new hard drive in a Windows computer. At first the operating system cannot see it. The airman partitions the drive, and the new partition appears with a drive letter; then the airman formats it with a file system so files can be stored and retrieved.
1.example: A new notebook gets section tabs before anyone writes in it, so each subject has its own place. Partitioning gives a drive its sections. In the course: partitioning is the process of dividing the physical hard drive into smaller units called partitions, Study Guide p.25.

1.summary: The Master Boot Record (MBR) is a legacy disk partitioning system that allows four partitions per disk and at most 2TB of combined storage.
1.deeper:
MBR is supported by every major operating system, including Microsoft Windows. It allows a maximum of only four partitions per disk, and the combined storage space of all partitions cannot exceed 2TB; on a larger disk, the disk still works, but only 2TB of storage is available. The first sector of an MBR disk contains the Master Boot Record, which tells BIOS where to find the operating system so the computer can boot, and the partition table, which describes the number and size of partitions on the disk.

Primary partition: MBR can create two types of partitions, primary and extended. Windows must be installed on a primary partition because it can't boot from an extended partition. An MBR disk can have up to four primary partitions, or up to three primary partitions and one extended partition. If more than four partitions are needed, the extended partition can be divided into multiple logical partitions; Windows gives every primary and logical partition its own drive letter.

The newer GUID Partition Table (GPT) overcomes these limits but needs UEFI.
1.analogy: An MBR disk is like a building lot with room for four houses. One plot can instead hold an apartment block (the extended partition) with many flats inside (logical partitions). The owner, Windows, must live in a house, a primary partition, not in a flat.
1.scenario: An airman partitions an MBR disk and needs five partitions. Windows goes on a primary partition. To get past four, the airman creates three primary partitions and one extended partition, then divides the extended partition into logical partitions.
1.example: The first page of a binder often holds a table of contents that says where each section starts. The first sector of an MBR disk does that for its partitions and the OS. In the course: the first sector of an MBR disk contains the Master Boot Record, which tells BIOS where to find the operating system so the computer can boot up, Study Guide p.26.

1.summary: The GUID Partition Table (GPT) is a newer disk partitioning system that numbers each partition with a long random string, almost certainly unique.
1.deeper:
GUID stands for globally unique identifier: each partition is numbered with a random string of characters so lengthy that it is almost certainly unique in the whole universe. GPT allows a vast number of partitions on a single disk, though Windows imposes a maximum of 128 GPT partitions. GPT also overcomes the 2TB size limit of the Master Boot Record (MBR), supporting drives up to 9.4ZB.

GPT partitions a disk using Logical Block Addressing (LBA) rather than the legacy Cylinder-Head-Sector scheme used by MBR. GPT is a subset of the UEFI specification, so it can only be used with modern motherboards with UEFI enabled. MBR, the legacy system, allows only four partitions per disk and 2TB of combined storage.
1.analogy: MBR is like a parking lot with four marked spaces and a fence around it. GPT is a huge lot where every space gets its own long serial number, so no two spaces are ever confused. The huge lot only opens to cars with a newer pass, UEFI.
1.scenario: An airman prepares a disk larger than 2TB on a modern computer with UEFI enabled. MBR would leave only 2TB usable, so the airman uses GPT, which overcomes that limit and allows many more partitions.
1.example: Every new car gets a vehicle number so long that no two cars share it. GPT numbers each partition the same way. In the course: GPT is a newer disk partitioning system in which each partition is numbered with a random string of characters, Study Guide p.26.

1.summary: A file system is the structure a partition is formatted with so the disk can store and retrieve data in an organized manner.
1.deeper:
A newly installed drive is like an empty file cabinet with no dividers, folders or labels. To make it useful it must be conditioned: partitioned and then formatted. Partitioning comes first and makes the drive visible to the operating system. After a hard disk drive (HDD) is partitioned, it must be formatted with a suitable file system.

The file system lets the disk store and retrieve data in an organized manner. It also provides essential utilities, such as the CREATE, DELETE, CUT, COPY, PASTE and RENAME commands, so a user can manage files, and it stores metadata about each file, such as the date created, the date of last edit, the date of last access, and the file size and type. The three most common file systems used with Windows are FAT32, exFAT and NTFS.
1.analogy: If the drive is an empty file cabinet, partitioning puts in the drawers and the file system adds the folders, labels and index cards, so every paper can be filed and found again.
1.scenario: An airman installs a new HDD. First the airman partitions it so Windows can see it; then the partition is formatted with a file system such as NTFS. Only then can the airman create, copy and rename files on it.
1.example: A library shelf holds books, but the catalogue lets you find one. A file system is the catalogue for a disk. In the course: a file system allows a disk to store and retrieve data in an organized manner, Study Guide p.26.

1.summary: FAT32 is a legacy, lightweight Microsoft file system with basic file management commands and no advanced features such as encryption or compression.
1.deeper:
FAT32 was introduced with Windows 95. FAT stands for File Allocation Table, and 32 refers to the 32-bit architecture used to specify logical sectors on a disk. It is supported by every major operating system and is still very popular for USB flash drives, SD cards and other portable media; it works with virtually anything that has a USB port.

FAT32 is simple and lightweight: it supports a basic set of commands for file management but offers no advanced features such as file encryption or data compression. A FAT32 partition can be no larger than 8TB, and no individual file can be larger than 4GB. NTFS, by contrast, adds advanced features such as journaling, permissions, quotas, compression, encryption, sharing, partition resizing and bad sector mapping, and Windows must be installed on an NTFS partition. exFAT was released in 2006 to replace FAT32 on portable media without its size limits.
1.analogy: FAT32 is like a plain paper notebook: anyone can read it anywhere, but it has no lock and no way to shrink what is written in it. NTFS is the office binder system with locks, logs and limits.
1.scenario: An airman needs a USB flash drive that every computer, camera and TV in the office can read. FAT32 suits the job because every major operating system supports it, as long as no single file is larger than 4GB and nothing needs encryption.
1.example: A simple key ring works with every lock it was cut for but offers no alarm. FAT32 works almost everywhere but offers no advanced features. In the course: FAT32 is simple and lightweight, supporting a basic set of commands for file management but no advanced features such as file encryption or data compression, Study Guide p.27.

1.summary: Extended File Allocation Table (exFAT) is a Microsoft file system for USB flash drives, SD cards and other portable media, without the size limits of FAT32.
1.deeper:
exFAT, also called FAT64, is a proprietary file system released by Microsoft in 2006 as a replacement for FAT32. Like FAT32 it is optimized for USB flash drives, SD cards and other portable media, but it does not have FAT32's limits of 4GB per file and 8TB per partition. The SD association has adopted exFAT as the standard for SD cards larger than 32GB.

exFAT is not yet as popular as FAT32, but it is widely supported by many software and hardware vendors. It is one of the three most common file systems used with Windows, with FAT32 and NTFS. The Windows operating system itself must be installed on an NTFS partition, not on exFAT.
1.analogy: FAT32 is like a suitcase that will not take any single item longer than a set size. exFAT is the newer suitcase from the same maker, built for travel, that takes the long items too.
1.scenario: An airman must copy a single file larger than 4GB onto a USB flash drive. FAT32 cannot hold a file that large, so the airman formats the drive with exFAT, which is made for portable media without that limit.
1.example: When a family outgrows a small car, it buys a bigger model of the same kind, still easy to park. exFAT is that bigger model of FAT32 for portable media. In the course: exFAT is a proprietary file system released by Microsoft in 2006 as a replacement for FAT32, Study Guide p.27.

1.summary: New Technology File System (NTFS) is a proprietary Microsoft file system, released in 1993 for Windows NT 3.1, that adds many advanced features not available with FAT file systems; Windows must be installed on an NTFS partition.
1.deeper:
NTFS supports a maximum partition size and file size of 256TB as implemented by Windows. Besides the basic utilities for file management and metadata, it offers advanced features: permissions (an access list that controls which users have access to which files, with access levels such as ACCESS DENIED, READ ONLY or READ AND WRITE), compression (to save disk space, at a possible cost of slower processing), encryption (on the Professional or Server Edition of Windows), sharing of files and folders over a network, partition resizing (expanding or shrinking a partition without reformatting the disk or reinstalling Windows), and bad sector mapping, so that Windows does not try to use bad sectors. FAT32, by contrast, has only a basic set of commands and no advanced features such as file encryption or data compression.

NTFS journaling: NTFS maintains a running record (journal) of file changes, which allows files to be recovered in the event of a power failure or system crash.

NTFS quotas: NTFS lets the administrator set storage limits that prevent any one user from using up all the disk space.
1.analogy: NTFS is like a well-run storeroom rather than an open closet: a log book records every change, a key list says who may open which shelf, and each person gets a fixed amount of shelf space.
1.scenario: An airman sets up a shared drive on a Windows computer that several people use. NTFS lets the administrator build an access list so only the right users reach each folder, set quotas so no one user fills the disk, and later grow the partition without reformatting. If the power fails, its journal helps recover the files.
1.example: A bank account keeps a running record of every deposit and withdrawal, so the balance can be rebuilt after a problem. NTFS keeps such a record of file changes, along with its other advanced features. In the course: NTFS supports many advanced features not available with FAT file systems, Study Guide p.27.

1.summary: A solid-state drive (SSD) is a data storage device that uses solid-state (flash) memory to store persistent, nonvolatile data, giving access just like a traditional hard disk drive (HDD) but with no moving parts.
1.deeper: There are two major types of storage drives: platter-based and solid state. Platter-based HDDs are electromechanical devices that use spinning magnetic platters and movable read/write heads. SSDs, in contrast, use integrated circuits that retain data in non-volatile memory chips and contain no moving parts. Compared with electromechanical HDDs, SSDs are typically more resistant to physical shock, are silent, and have faster access and read/write times. The fast SSD is the expensive one and the HDD the cheaper but slower one; a hybrid drive combines flash memory and platters to bridge that gap. An SSD can use the same SATA interface as an HDD.
1.analogy: An HDD is like a record player: a disc spins and an arm moves to the right spot before anything can be read. An SSD is like a printed page you can read at a glance: nothing has to move first.
1.scenario: An airman's laptop is carried into the field and often gets bumped. The airman replaces its platter-based HDD with an SSD: with no spinning platters or moving heads, it stands up better to physical shock, runs silent and gives faster access.
1.example: A music box plays by turning a drum, while a phone plays the same song from chips with nothing turning. An SSD stores data like the phone, with no moving parts. In the course: SSDs use integrated circuits which retain data in non-volatile memory chips and contain no moving parts, Study Guide p.29.

1.summary: A hybrid drive combines flash memory and spinning platters in one drive, putting the most important, performance-sensitive data on the flash memory.
1.deeper:
There are two major types of storage drive: platter-based hard disk drives (HDDs), which use magnetic platters, and solid-state drives (SSDs), which use integrated circuits. A hybrid drive combines flash memory and a platter-based hard drive into a single drive. It bridges the gap between the expensive but fast SSD and the cheaper but slower HDD.

Computers that use a hybrid drive keep their more important or performance-sensitive data on the flash memory portion for faster access, and use the spinning platters for bulk storage.
1.analogy: A hybrid drive is like a desk with a small top drawer and a large cabinet below. The papers you use all the time stay in the drawer, close at hand; everything else goes into the big, slower cabinet.
1.scenario: An airman's computer has a hybrid drive. The data it uses most, the performance-sensitive data, sits on the flash memory portion for fast access, while large files sit on the spinning platters for bulk storage.
1.example: A kitchen keeps everyday spices on the counter and bulk supplies in the pantry. A hybrid drive keeps everyday data on flash memory and bulk data on platters. In the course: hybrid drives combine flash memory and platter-based hard drives into a single drive, Study Guide p.29.

1.summary: A Digital Versatile Disc (DVD) is an optical disc that looks like a CD and fits the same drive, but its smaller, tighter pits and lands hold much more data.
1.deeper:
A DVD, also known as Digital Video Disc, works much like a CD: both shine a laser beam onto the surface of the disc to read pits that have been encoded on it. The DVD has a much larger storage capacity for several reasons. Its pits and lands are much smaller and packed closer together than those on a CD. To read them, a DVD drive uses a 650nm red laser, while a CD drive uses a 780nm red laser; the shorter wavelength lets the optics resolve much smaller details. The track that spirals out from the centre of the disc is much tighter, so the DVD player needs greater mechanical and optical precision and a far more precise tracking system.

There is another reason: a CD needs lots of extra error correction code to reduce read errors, and that code takes up a lot of storage space; newer error correction methods let a DVD pack even more onto the same size disc. A DVD can also be single sided/single layer, single sided/double layer, or double sided/double layer.
1.analogy: A CD and a DVD are like two pages of the same size: one written in large handwriting with wide lines, the other in small, neat print on tight lines. The second page holds far more, but you need sharper eyes to read it.
1.scenario: An airman compares two discs that look exactly alike and fit the same drive. One holds much more than the other. The DVD packs smaller pits and lands closer together on a tighter spiral track, read by a shorter 650nm red laser, and can even use two layers or two sides.
1.example: Writing smaller and closer lets one page carry more words. A DVD carries more data the same way. In the course: DVD discs look exactly like compact discs and fit in the same drive, but they have a much larger storage capacity, Study Guide p.31.

1.summary: A Blu-ray disc is a high-capacity optical disc for storing digital information, including high-definition video; its blue-violet laser lets it hold far more data than a DVD.
1.deeper: Blu-ray works much like CD-ROM and DVD technology, and a Blu-ray disc fits into a standard CD/DVD drive. A fundamental difference is the type of laser used to read and write the data on the disc: the "Blu-ray" name comes from the 405nm wavelength blue-violet laser. Because of the laser's shorter wavelength, the optics can resolve smaller pits and lands that are more densely packed, so substantially more data fits on a Blu-ray disc. A single layer Blu-ray disc can store 25GB, over 5 times the size of a single layer 4.7GB DVD, and a dual layer disc 50GB, almost 6 times a dual layer DVD at 8.5GB. About 9 hours of high-definition video fits on a 50GB disc. For comparison, a DVD drive uses a 650nm red laser and a CD-ROM drive a 780nm red laser.
1.analogy: A Blu-ray laser is like a finer pen: the finer the tip, the smaller the letters it can write and read, and the more words fit on the same page.
1.scenario: An airman needs to store high-definition video on one optical disc. A single layer DVD holds 4.7GB; a single layer Blu-ray disc holds 25GB, because its blue-violet laser can read smaller, more densely packed pits and lands. The airman chooses the Blu-ray disc.

1.summary: A magnetic tape drive reads and writes on magnetic tape in sequential format; it is seldom used on personal computers but still used for enterprise network data backup.
1.deeper:
Magnetic tape is a storage medium: it holds data until the system is ready to use it, and output data can be stored on tape for later use. It offers high resistance to physical shock and an extremely long data retention shelf-life compared to other storage media. Data on tape can be read repeatedly without being destroyed, but writing new information over old information destroys the old. Stray magnetic fields can destroy the data, and temperature and humidity can affect the tape, so storage areas are usually temperature and humidity controlled.

All tape systems have a major disadvantage: the data is stored in sequential format. If the tape is at the beginning of the reel and the desired data is at the end, the entire tape must pass under the read head before the data can be read. This is known as sequential access, and it can cause lengthy access time.
1.analogy: A tape is like a long scroll: to read the last line you must unroll everything before it. A book with page numbers, by contrast, lets you jump straight to the page you want.
1.scenario: An airman restores a file from an enterprise backup tape. The tape is rewound to the start of the reel, and the file is at the end, so the drive must run the whole tape past the read head before the file can be read.
1.example: A song near the end of an old cassette can only be reached by winding through everything before it. Tape storage works the same way. In the course: the data is stored in sequential format, and it may take considerable time to locate the desired data, Study Guide p.33.

1.summary: Flash memory is non-volatile memory that stores each one or zero as a small electric charge held in a cell.
1.deeper:
In flash memory, information is stored in cells, each holding a one or a zero, as the presence or absence of a small electric charge on the gate of a floating-gate transistor. Its underlying technology is basically the same as ROM: flash memory is a type of EEPROM. Accessing the cells is slow compared to regular RAM, and blocks of memory must be erased all at once; a programmed byte must be erased before it can be changed.

Its major benefit is that it is non-volatile, which makes it perfect for devices that use batteries, such as digital cameras, tablet computers and smartphones. Flash memory is also silent, allows faster access, is smaller and lighter, and has no moving parts. Two factors keep it from replacing everything: it costs more per GB than a hard disk drive, and only a limited number of read/write operations can be performed, so it wears out. Examples include a computer BIOS chip, CompactFlash, Secure Digital (SD) cards and USB flash drives.
1.analogy: Flash memory is like a notebook written in ink: what is written stays even when the lamp goes off, but each page can only be erased and rewritten so many times before it wears thin.
1.scenario: An airman picks storage for a battery-powered tablet. Flash memory keeps its data without power, is silent, small and light and has no moving parts, so it fits. The trade-offs are a higher cost per GB than a hard disk drive and a limited number of read/write operations.
1.example: A light switch stays where you put it until someone changes it; it does not need power to remember its position. A flash cell keeps its one or zero the same way. In the course: in flash memory, information is stored in cells with each cell holding a one or zero, Study Guide p.34.

1.summary: A video card (also called a graphics accelerator card, display adapter or graphics adapter) is a computer hardware component whose function is to generate output images to a monitor; it is a separate expansion card plugged into a PCI slot on the motherboard.
1.deeper:
Video cards give the computer the means to "talk" to the monitor so it can display what the computer is doing. The term video card means a separate, dedicated expansion card, as opposed to a graphics controller integrated into the motherboard chipset or the CPU itself. It consists of a printed circuit board with mounted components, including a Video BIOS chip with the basic I/O program that governs its operations, and it connects to the display through one of several connection systems.

Graphics Processing Unit (GPU): a dedicated microprocessor on the card that lightens the workload of the computer's CPU.

Video Random Access Memory (VRAM): RAM used specifically for video adapters, located on the graphics card to free up system RAM; the amount of VRAM is a determining factor in the resolution and color depth of the display.

Random Access Memory Digital-to-Analog Converter (RAMDAC): responsible for turning the digital signals produced by the GPU into analog signals for the monitor.

SVGA connection: an analog standard designed for CRT displays, with problems of electrical noise, image distortion and sampling error; it is legacy, though many computers and monitors still have SVGA connectors.

DVI connection: designed for digital displays such as LCDs, plasma screens and video projectors; it reduces image distortion and electrical noise.

Component video: three cables, each with an RCA connector; used in projectors.

High-Definition Multimedia Interface (HDMI): an all-digital audio/video interface capable of transmitting uncompressed streams, whose goal is to replace all the other connections.
1.analogy: A video card is like an interpreter between the computer and the monitor: the GPU works out what to say, the memory on the card spares the computer's own memory, and a cable carries the message in a form the monitor understands.
1.scenario: An airman connects an older CRT monitor to a computer with a video card. The GPU produces the image as digital signals, the RAMDAC turns them into analog signals, and the SVGA connection carries them to the CRT display. A new LCD at the next desk uses a DVI or HDMI connection instead.
1.example: A projector at a briefing takes a laptop's slides and puts them on the screen for everyone to see. A video card is the part that puts a computer's output on its monitor. 1.summary: A network interface card (NIC) is a circuit card installed in a computer that allows it to connect to a network and interface with other computers; it provides a dedicated, full-time connection to a network.
1.deeper:
The network interface may be integral to the motherboard or a separate, dedicated card installed in an internal expansion slot; small adapters can also convert a USB port into a wired Ethernet or wireless Wi-Fi connection. In any case the NIC has a unique MAC address that identifies the network adapter in the system. The back plate of the NIC typically features a hardware port called an RJ-45, which accommodates an Ethernet cable. NICs are available for many kinds of bound media, including optical fiber, coaxial copper cable and twisted-pair copper cable. A NIC can also support a wireless (Wi-Fi) connection: a wireless card is installed just like a wired one, but in place of a port for an Ethernet cable it features a small antenna, and it communicates with the central wireless switch (Wireless Access Point) by radio waves. A NIC is both an OSI layer 1 (physical) and layer 2 (data link) device.

Network switch: the Ethernet cable connects each NIC to a central device called a switch. The switch acts like a relay, passing information between computers using the MAC addresses, so resources like printers, scanners and media servers can be shared.
1.analogy: A NIC is like the front door of a house onto the street: it is the computer's own fixed way out to the network, and the street (the cable) leads to a junction (the switch) that connects every house.
1.scenario: An airman moves a desktop to a new desk. The airman plugs an Ethernet cable into the RJ-45 port on the back of the computer's NIC and runs it to the switch, which relays traffic to the other computers and the shared printer. A laptop nearby uses a wireless NIC with an antenna instead of a cable.
1.example: A phone jack in the wall gives a house a full-time line to the phone network. A NIC gives a computer a full-time line to its network. In the course: network interface cards provide a dedicated, full-time connection to a network, Study Guide p.37.

1.summary: A Media Access Control (MAC) address is the unique, 12-digit (48-bit) hexadecimal number that identifies a network interface card (NIC) in the system.
1.deeper:
Every NIC, whether built into the motherboard, on an expansion card or on a USB adapter, has a MAC address burned into it. MAC address is synonymous with physical address and hardware address. No two NICs on the same network can share the same MAC address, so the unique MAC addresses are used to identify and address traffic to each local area network (LAN) node: a computer, printer, media server or smart TV. The switch that each NIC's Ethernet cable connects to passes information between computers using these MAC addresses. A NIC is an OSI layer 2 (data link layer) device because it provides a low-level addressing system using MAC addresses, and MAC addresses are easily discovered using simple command line tools.

Do not confuse a MAC address with an I/O port address. An I/O port address is also a hexadecimal number that no two devices can share, but it is a memory address the processor uses for direct communication with a device that has sent an interrupt signal, and many devices use a range of them.
1.analogy: A MAC address is like the serial number stamped into a part at the factory: it is fixed in the part itself, and it lets anyone tell that part apart from every other one on the same shelf.
1.scenario: An airman connects a computer and a printer to the same switch. Each one has its own NIC, and each NIC has its own MAC address. When the computer sends a print job, the switch uses the printer's MAC address to pass the traffic to the printer's NIC and to no other node.
1.example: Every car carries its own identification number, set when it is built, and no two cars share one; that number tells exactly which car is which. A MAC address does the same for each network adapter. In the course: the NIC has a unique, 12-digit (48-bit) hexadecimal number called a Media Access Control (MAC) address that identifies the Network Adapter in the system, Study Guide p.37.

1.summary: Device drivers are the software components of hardware devices; they let those devices communicate with the operating system (OS).
1.deeper:
The OS must recognize every hardware device, and a device driver is what lets a device communicate with the OS. That is why installing the most current driver is a vital part of the hardware installation process: if the wrong driver is installed, the hardware component or I/O device may not function properly.

Most device drivers come on a CD-ROM or other media with the device, and the vendor typically releases driver updates on its product support website. Occasionally an update will not install or function properly; then a Windows machine can be rolled back to use the previous drivers, an option found in Device Manager. A device that is not on the Hardware Compatibility List (HCL) may have an unverified or unsigned driver, and there is no guarantee that an unsigned driver will function.

A device driver is a type of system software: it is essential to the functioning of computer hardware but has no interaction with the human user.
1.analogy: A device driver is like an interpreter between a visitor and a host who speak different languages. Without the right interpreter the two cannot work together, and the wrong interpreter leaves them stuck. If a new interpreter gets it wrong, you call the old one back.
1.scenario: An airman installs a new device on a Windows computer and loads the most current driver from the vendor's product support website. Later a driver update does not function properly, so the airman uses Device Manager to roll back to the previous driver, and the device works again.
1.example: A new appliance comes with its own instructions so the house wiring and the appliance work together. A device driver plays that part between a device and the OS. In the course: device drivers are the software components of hardware devices and allow devices to communicate with the OS, Study Guide p.40.

1.summary: Universal Serial Bus (USB) is an industry standard for personal computers and peripheral devices, with standardized ports, electronics, connectors, cables and protocols; it provides communication and/or electrical power to compatible connected devices.
1.deeper:
The original goal of USB was to make computers easier to use by replacing the confusing multitude of serial ports, keyboard and mouse ports and printer ports with a single, standard connector port. USB was first introduced in 1996 and keeps evolving in speed and usefulness; newer versions are backward-compatible with older ones. Because USB supports such a wide variety of devices, they are divided into 21 distinct classes, each identified by a specific class code. Human Interface Device (HiD), class 03h, includes keyboards, mice, joysticks and game controllers: devices that let a human interact with the computer. Mass Storage Class (MSC), class 08h, supports flash drives, memory cards, digital audio players, digital cameras and external hard drives. USB also uses electrical protocols to provide DC power to bus powered devices such as mice, keyboards and portable hard drives.

Universal Serial Bus host controller: an integrated circuit built into the motherboard chipset that controls every USB device connected to it. It supports communication and DC power to connected devices through a root hub, which in turn connects to the external ports.
1.analogy: USB is like a universal power strip that takes one standard plug: instead of a different socket for every appliance, every device uses the same kind of port.
1.scenario: An airman connects a keyboard, a mouse and an external hard drive to one computer, all through the same kind of USB port. The keyboard and mouse belong to the Human Interface Device class (03h), and the external hard drive to the Mass Storage Class (08h). The host controller in the chipset controls all three.
1.example: A standard wall outlet lets a lamp, a fan and a phone charger all plug into the same kind of socket. USB gives computer devices one standard port in the same way. In the course: the original goal of USB was to make computers easier to use by replacing the confusing multitude of serial ports, keyboard & mouse ports, and printer ports with a single, standard connector port, Study Guide p.41.

1.summary: The USB root hub is the part of the USB host controller that makes the physical connection to the external USB ports; it is really a bus, like an expansion bus.
1.deeper: The USB host controller, built into the motherboard chipset, supports communication and DC power to connected devices through the root hub, and the root hub in turn connects to the external ports. In theory, a root hub can support up to 127 connected devices. In practice, connecting 127 devices to a single root hub is a bad idea: every device connected to a root hub shares the bus with every other connected device. The more devices you connect, the slower the bus and the greater the DC power demand.
1.analogy: A root hub is like one hallway that every room opens onto: the more people use the hallway at once, the slower everyone moves, and the more lighting and heating it needs.
1.scenario: An airman's desk computer has a keyboard, a mouse, two external drives, a phone charging and a webcam all on the same root hub, and the drives seem slow. Every device shares the root hub's bus, so the more that are connected, the slower the bus and the greater the DC power demand.
1.example: One water main feeding a whole street gives each house less pressure as more taps are opened at the same time. A root hub's bus is shared the same way. In the course: every device connected to a root hub shares the bus with every other connected device, Study Guide p.41.

1.summary: A heat sink is a metal component or assembly that transfers and dissipates heat from a hot chip in a solid material.
1.deeper:
CPUs and graphics processors use heat sinks because of the heat their chips generate. Heat sinks are made of metals that are good conductors of heat, such as aluminum, copper or brass. A typical heat sink has a large, flat area for good thermal coupling with the hot component, plus an array of fins to increase surface area. The big crown of fins is not for decoration: their large surface area enhances heat transfer to the air by radiation and convection.

Thermal paste: air is a poor conductor of heat, so thermal paste (also known as thermal compound) is added to the base of the heat sink to help thermal conduction between the CPU and the heat sink. It fills the gap between the two objects, including all the microscopic imperfections that can trap air, for better heat transfer; it can be 100 times more efficient than air at removing heat from a CPU.

Many modern components also need active cooling: a fan is usually mounted right on top of the CPU heat sink.
1.analogy: A heat sink is like a radiator with many thin ribs: heat spreads into the metal and leaves through the wide surface of the ribs. Thermal paste is like the grease that makes two parts sit snugly, so no air pockets block the way.
1.scenario: An airman reseats a CPU heat sink. Before mounting it, the airman adds thermal paste to its base, because air trapped in tiny gaps would block heat. The heat then flows from the CPU into the metal base and out through the fins to the air.
1.example: A metal cooking pan spreads the heat of a burner across its whole surface. A heat sink spreads a chip's heat the same way, then gives it to the air. In the course: a heat sink is a component or assembly that transfers and dissipates heat in a solid material, Study Guide p.46.

1.summary: Active cooling uses fans to move heated air away from a computer's internal components and draw cooler air over them; many modern components need it.
1.deeper: Earlier personal computers cooled most components using natural convection, called passive cooling. Many modern components require more effective active cooling methods: modern computers use fans to move heated air away from internal components and draw cooler air over them. The CPU usually has a fan mounted right on top of its heat sink, and video cards often have one or more small cooling fans attached. Case fans ventilate the computer case: some draw cool outside air in through the front of the case and force the internal hot air out through the rear; some use a rear case fan to pull the hot air out, which draws in cool air through other openings in the case. Combinations of front, rear and side case fans can improve cooling, and high performance cases may have a fan in front of the drive bay to keep the hard drives cool. For all this to work properly, all open slots must have their covers in place. For high-end hardware, liquid cooling (water-cooling) can be a better solution, because cooling with water is far more effective than cooling with air.
1.analogy: Active cooling is like a room with one window fan blowing in and another blowing out: cool air comes in on one side, passes over everyone in the room, and the warm air is pushed out the other side. Passive cooling is the same room with the windows open and no fans.
1.scenario: An airman opens a desktop case and finds a fan on top of the CPU's heat sink, small fans on the video card, a front case fan and a rear case fan. Before closing the case, the airman makes sure every open slot has its cover in place, so the case fans can draw cool air in through the front and force the hot air out through the rear.
1.example: A desk fan on a hot day moves the warm air away from you and brings cooler air across you. In the course: modern computers use fans to move heated air away from internal components and draw cooler air over them, Study Guide p.47.

1.term: Department of the Air Force Manual
1.summary: The Department of the Air Force Manual (DAFMAN) 17-1203, Information Technology Asset Management, governs software use in the Air Force.
1.deeper:
DAFMAN 17-1203 gives guidance and direction for the operational management of information technology (IT) hardware and software. It applies to Air Force-procured commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) software, such as Microsoft Office, and to software developed for unique Air Force purposes. It does not apply to software that is internal to or integrated into a weapon system.

Responsibility for software license management rises to the highest levels of Air Force leadership: the Chief Information Officer (SAF/CN) is the top software license manager for the entire USAF, and Air Combat Command (ACC) is the lead command for software license management. The question to ask about any copyrighted software is whether its use complies with public law and Air Force Instructions, and whether it is installed and used in a manner compatible with the terms of its license.
1.analogy: DAFMAN 17-1203 is like the rule book of a sports league. The rule book says how the game is run; the league office (SAF/CN) sits at the top, and one lead team (ACC) leads license management. Games played on a different field, such as weapon systems, are outside this rule book.

The answer starts with one publication, DAFMAN 17-1203, which covers the COTS software the Air Force buys and the software it develops for its own purposes. Above it all, SAF/CN is the top software license manager, and ACC leads software license management.

1.summary: An enterprise license lets the purchasing organization use multiple copies of a specific COTS software program, usually up to a specified number, for a set price.
1.deeper:
An enterprise license covers the whole organization: many copies of one commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) program, usually up to a specified number, for a set price. It is usually a more cost-effective acquisition strategy than buying individual copies. For commonly used software, either the Air Force Enterprise Software License Program or the Department of Defense (DOD) Enterprise Software Initiative (ESI) should be considered. Enterprise software agreement (ESA): agreements, such as contracts or blanket purchase agreements, by which organizations acquire software or software maintenance under specified terms and conditions. An enterprise license is about how many copies may be used for one price; an ESA is the agreement by which the software or its maintenance is acquired.
