1.summary: The DoDIN Approved Product List (APL) is the list of all software approved for use on Air Force networks; before using any COTS software, you must ensure it is on the list.
1.deeper:
Applications on Air Force networks must be thoroughly vetted and tested to ensure they are free of malware and security vulnerabilities, and they must be stable, reliable and compatible with other software products: a faulty application could destroy valuable information if it failed across the entire AFNET. One of the essential tools for any CST is the Department of Defense Information Network (DoDIN) Approved Product List (APL), the list of all the software approved for use on Air Force networks, including any COTS software that has been purchased. It was established to identify products that have undergone security and interoperability testing, so Military Departments and DoD agencies can acquire and deploy them. Before using any COTS software, you must ensure it has been approved for use on an Air Force network.

Approved Products Certification Office: the APL process is managed by the Defense Information Systems Agency's (DISA) Approved Products Certification Office (APCO).

Software certification: before a product is added to the APL, it must undergo rigorous testing and certification at a DoD operated lab, a process that can take 13-15 months. Certification is the act of determining that software performs without defects and viruses and does what the supporting documentation says it will do, in accordance with any specified acceptance criteria.

Security Technical Implementation Guides: the first category of APL testing, Cybersecurity (CS) or Information Assurance (IA) testing, proves that the product can be securely configured based on the DoD provided Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIGs).

Interoperability testing: the second category, Interoperability (IO) testing, ensures that the product operates correctly when placed in the DoD network.
1.analogy: The APL is like a list of foods a dining hall has already inspected: a cook may serve only what is on the list, and each item got there by passing the inspector's safety checks and showing it works in that kitchen.
1.scenario: An airman is asked to put a purchased COTS program on an Air Force workstation. Before using it, the airman checks the DoDIN APL. The program is listed, which means it passed testing and certification at a DoD operated lab, including cybersecurity testing against the STIGs and interoperability testing.
1.example: A school may let students bring only the calculators on its approved list, each one checked before the exam. In the course: The DoDIN Approved Product List is a list of all the software that has been approved for use on Air Force networks, Study Guide p.50.

2.summary: A computer is composed of two main components, hardware and software; hardware is the physical part of the computer that does the work, such as a hard disk drive.
2.deeper:
Hardware is the physical part of the computer which does the work. A hard disk drive (HDD) is an example of hardware.

Software is the other main component: a collection of data or instructions that tell the computer how to work. It consists of lines of code written in one of many programming languages, so it is easily modified as needed; it is also easily corrupted, either accidentally or deliberately. Its two broad types are system software, such as the OS, and application software, such as Adobe.

The two work together: the file system and device drivers that make the hard disk drive useful are examples of software, while the drive itself is hardware.
2.analogy: Hardware is like a piano and software is like the sheet music: the piano is the physical thing that makes the sound, and the music tells it what to play. Pages of music are easy to rewrite or spoil; the piano stays the same.
2.scenario: An airman holds a hard disk drive: that physical part is hardware. The file system that organizes its files and the device drivers that let the computer use it are software, lines of code that tell the computer how to work and that can be easily modified or corrupted.
2.example: A car is the machine that does the driving; the route in its navigation system only tells it where to go. In the course: hardware is the physical part of the computer which does the work, Study Guide p.52.

2.summary: An operating system is system software that provides a platform for application software to run, provides the instructions and drivers that make the hardware operate, and is the bridge between the human user and the computer hardware.
2.deeper:
Because the OS is the bridge between the human user and the computer hardware, it determines the quality of the overall user experience: a fast, intuitive, easy OS makes users productive; a buggy, slow, hard one makes them unproductive. Its expected features include a graphical user interface, a command prompt, security (password protection, file encryption and limited user versus administrator privileges that prevent unauthorized configuration changes), a file system (directories and folders, user files kept apart from system files, and a search function), networking, updates, the kernel and program execution.

Graphical user interface (GUI): the desktop environment, window manager, language, icon set, character set, fonts, theme, task bar and application menu that the user works with by mouse, keyboard and/or touch screen. The GUI makes the computer easy to use by hiding hardware and software complexity from the user.

Command prompt feature: lets the user input text-only commands to the computer with a keyboard. Most user and administrator tasks can be done through the GUI, but sometimes only a command prompt will do. Windows CMD and the Linux terminal are examples of OS utilities that provide one; PowerShell and Terminal are others.
2.analogy: An operating system is like an interpreter between a visitor and a machine shop: the visitor speaks either by pointing at pictures (the GUI) or by typing exact orders (the command prompt), and the interpreter turns both into work the machines can do.
2.scenario: An airman uses the desktop, icons and menus of a workstation's GUI for most tasks. One maintenance task can be done only by typing text commands, so she opens a command prompt. Her password and limited user privileges are OS security features, and the file system keeps her files apart from system files.
2.example: A car's dashboard lets a driver use the engine without seeing how it works. In the course: the operating system is the bridge between the human user and the computer hardware, Study Guide p.52.

2.summary: The kernel is the very core of the operating system; it loads first when the OS starts up and provides the most basic level of control over all the computer's hardware devices.
2.deeper: Much of the kernel code consists of hardware device drivers. The primary responsibility of the kernel is computer resource management, in three areas. CPU control and access: the kernel decides which of the many running programs should be allocated to the CPU for processing at any given time. RAM allocation and access: the kernel allocates memory (RAM) to running programs. Input/Output (I/O) devices: disk drives, keyboard, printer, mouse, network adapters (NIC) and display hardware.
2.analogy: The kernel is like a dispatcher at a busy depot: it starts work before anyone else arrives, decides which job gets the one forklift next, hands out parking spaces, and handles every door and radio.
2.scenario: An airman starts a workstation and opens several programs. The kernel loaded first, as the OS started. Now it decides which program is allocated the CPU at each moment, allocates RAM to each running program, and handles the keyboard, mouse, printer and disk drives.
2.example: An air traffic controller decides which aircraft uses the one runway next. In the course: the kernel is the very core of the OS and loads first when the OS starts up, Study Guide p.53.

2.summary: BIOS is not an operating system: although it provides drivers, a user interface and some security, its fundamental purpose is to turn the computer over to an operating system as soon as it is capable of booting.
2.deeper:
An operating system is a type of system software. BIOS consists of lines of code called firmware, which is necessary to wake up the computer when it is first booted. Firmware is stored on ROM, seldom needs updating, and provides basic hardware support for the computer during pre-boot.

BIOS has some things an OS has. The CMOS menu provides a user interface that lets the user adjust hardware settings, system time and date, boot priority and so on, and CMOS settings can be password protected to prevent unauthorized changes or access. BIOS also provides hardware device drivers. Even so, it does not qualify as an operating system, mainly because of its purpose: to hand the computer over to an OS as soon as the computer can boot. When the OS starts up, its kernel loads first and takes basic control of the hardware.
2.analogy: BIOS is like a tug that guides a ship out of the harbour: it has an engine and a crew, but its job is to hand the ship over to its own power as soon as it can sail. The OS is the ship's own engine.
2.scenario: An airman powers on a workstation. BIOS firmware wakes the computer up and gives basic hardware support; she could open the CMOS menu to change the boot priority. As soon as the computer can boot, BIOS turns it over to the operating system, whose kernel loads first.
2.example: A starter motor gets a car's engine turning and then stops while the engine runs the car. In the course: the fundamental purpose of BIOS is to turn the computer over to an operating system as soon as it is capable of booting, Study Guide p.54.

2.summary: Firmware is a kind of software: normally very small programs stored on a ROM chip, seldom updated, that provide only the most basic hardware functionality.
2.deeper:
BIOS consists of lines of code called firmware, and it uses these small software programs to turn the computer over to an operating system as soon as it is capable of booting. Firmware provides basic hardware support for the computer during pre-boot.

Firmware differs from other kinds of software in three ways. It is normally very small programs stored on a ROM (Read Only Memory) chip. It is seldom updated, while other software is regularly updated. And it provides only the most basic hardware functionality, such as having a video display during boot, whereas software drivers can take full advantage of hardware capabilities.
2.analogy: Firmware is like the pilot light of a gas heater: small, built in, rarely touched, and only enough to get things started. The full flame, and everything the heater can really do, comes later.
2.scenario: An airman powers on a workstation. Before the OS loads, a plain video display appears: that comes from firmware, small programs on a ROM chip. Once the OS is running, its software drivers take full advantage of the same display hardware, and those drivers get regular updates while the firmware seldom does.
2.example: A flashlight's simple on-off switch is built in and almost never changes, while an app on a phone gets new versions all the time. In the course: firmware is a kind of software, normally very small programs stored on a ROM chip, Study Guide p.54.

2.summary: Windows 10 and Windows 11, and every Windows version since Windows 2000, are based on the NT (New Technology) kernel, so Windows is no longer dependent on MSDOS.
2.deeper:
Windows is a lengthy product line of multitasking, graphical operating systems developed, marketed and sold by the Microsoft Corporation. Its first release was version 1.0 in 1985. Windows evolved through many generations to the Windows that most desktop and laptop computers use now, and every version since Windows 2000 is based on the NT (New Technology) kernel.

Microsoft Disk Operating System (MSDOS): an older operating system. Early versions of Windows were just a graphical shell on top of MSDOS, to hide its command prompt. Windows NT and Windows 2000 discarded MSDOS.

PowerShell prompt: many of the original MSDOS text commands are still available for maintenance and administrative purposes through the CMD prompt or the PowerShell prompt. Like CMD, PowerShell is a way to input text-only commands.
2.analogy: Early Windows was like a new front built onto an old house; later Windows was rebuilt on a new foundation (the NT kernel), but a back door from the old house (the command prompts) was kept for maintenance.
2.scenario: An airman maintains a Windows 11 workstation. It runs on the NT kernel and does not depend on MSDOS, unlike early Windows versions, which were a graphical shell on top of MSDOS. For one maintenance task she still types an original MSDOS text command at the PowerShell prompt.

2.summary: UNIX is a family of multitasking operating systems derived from the original AT&T UNIX, developed in the 1970s at Bell Labs Research Center; it is the parent of the majority of operating systems in use today.
2.deeper:
UNIX was originally intended for internal corporate use only. Various licensing agreements then allowed it to branch off into commercial, academic and home-use versions. UNIX has also inspired several UNIX-like operating systems that borrow ideas and features from the UNIX design philosophy, and it is the parent of the majority of operating systems in use today. It is a family of multitasking, multiuser systems.

The most popular versions of UNIX are free and open source, so anyone can modify or improve the source code to suit a particular purpose. This, plus the absence of restrictive (and expensive) licensing, led to its widespread adoption by industry and academia.

UNIX is rarely used on personal computers, but it is still popular for its original purpose as a development environment for computer programmers. It is also found on embedded devices, supercomputers, game consoles, enterprise servers, routers and other network infrastructure.
2.analogy: UNIX is like a grandparent in a family tree: it began in one household, its children moved out into many homes, and most of today's family carries its traits.
2.scenario: An airman reads that MacOS, Linux-based systems, iOS and Android are all UNIX-like. Tracing back, she finds that UNIX began at AT&T's Bell Labs Research Center in the 1970s for internal use, licensing let it branch into commercial, academic and home versions, and today it is the parent of most systems in use.
2.example: A family recipe first cooked in one kitchen can spread to many homes, each changing it a little. In the course: UNIX is the parent of the majority of operating systems in use today, Study Guide p.55.

2.summary: Open-source software has source code that anyone can modify or improve to suit a particular purpose; the most popular versions of UNIX are free and open source.
2.deeper:
Open source means the source code can be modified or improved by anyone to suit a particular purpose. For UNIX, this, plus the absence of restrictive (and expensive) licensing, led to its widespread adoption by industry and academia. Linux, ChromeOS and Android are open source too; Android's source code may be freely copied and distributed.

Closed-source software: Windows is the proprietary and closed-source property of the Microsoft Corporation. MacOS is also proprietary and closed source, and iOS code is closed source with some open-source components.

End-user license agreements: restrictive licensing and legally binding end-user license agreements (EULA) make it illegal to modify, improve or even view the Windows source code. So the difference is not only about changing code: under the Windows EULA, even looking at it is illegal.
2.analogy: Open-source software is like a community recipe anyone may copy and change; closed-source software is like a restaurant's secret recipe, with a contract that forbids you even to read it.

2.summary: MacOS is a family of graphical, UNIX-like, multiuser and multitasking operating systems developed and marketed by Apple Inc. for Macintosh desktop and laptop computers.
2.deeper:
MacOS was previously called Mac OS X and OS X. It is the second most widely used desktop OS after Microsoft Windows. It is based on UNIX and borrows features from Darwin OS and FreeBSD. The GUI, window manager and other desktop tools that give MacOS its distinctive look and feel are closed source and proprietary.

Darwin system from Apple: Darwin OS was developed by Apple, and MacOS borrows features from it, alongside FreeBSD. The two are not the same: FreeBSD is an open-source version of UNIX, while Darwin is Apple's own.
2.analogy: MacOS is like a house built on a well-known foundation, with some rooms copied from two other houses, but with a front and interior design that only its builder may use.

2.summary: Strictly speaking, Linux is only a kernel, not an OS; an operating system is built on the Linux kernel by adding a GUI, window manager, file manager, theming, icon set and so on.
2.deeper:
Linux refers to a vast family of multitasking, free and open-source, UNIX-like operating systems, but the name itself is the kernel. Familiar systems built on it include Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Red Hat, Android and ChromeOS; hundreds of Linux-based operating systems are deployed worldwide. The Linux kernel was created in 1991.

Other systems use other kernels: Windows 10 and Windows 11 are based on the NT (New Technology) kernel, and iOS is based on the Darwin XNU kernel.

Linux is not very popular for desktop and laptop computers, with the notable exception of Chromebook laptops, which all use ChromeOS. But much of the infrastructure of the Internet, including many cloud servers and public and private data centers, runs on Linux, and in 2020 all of the world's top 500 supercomputers used it. Android, based on the Linux kernel, had 87% of the mobile device market worldwide in 2019.
2.analogy: The Linux kernel is like an engine sold on its own: it runs, but it is not a car until a maker adds a body, seats and a dashboard. Different makers build different cars around the same engine.
2.scenario: An airman lists the systems in a unit: Android phones, ChromeOS Chromebooks, an Ubuntu server and Windows 10 workstations. The first three are all built on the Linux kernel, each with its own GUI and tools added; the Windows workstations are based on the NT kernel instead.
2.example: One engine model can power several different cars once each maker adds its own body. In the course: strictly speaking, Linux is only a kernel, not an OS, Study Guide p.55.

2.summary: ChromeOS is an open-source, UNIX-like OS developed by Google and based on the Linux kernel; it is designed so that both user data and applications are based in the cloud.
2.deeper:
ChromeOS is used on Chromebook laptop devices. Google announced the ChromeOS project in 2009, and the first Chromebook reached the market in 2011. The Chrome web browser is its primary user interface.

ChromeOS includes an integrated file manager and media player; all other apps are web apps. It can run Chrome apps and has access to Android apps in the Google Play Store. In 2013 it gained the ability to run Linux applications through a third-party script called Crouton, and in 2018 it gained that ability without Crouton.

Linux-based systems are not very popular on desktop and laptop computers; Chromebook laptops, which all use ChromeOS, are the notable exception.

2.summary: A mobile device is a client that can be held in the hand, employs a mobile OS, uses a touchscreen as the primary user interface and uses a wireless network connection such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or the cellular phone network.
2.deeper:
Mobile devices include smartphones, tablet computers, intermediate-sized devices (phablets) and digital book readers. Modern smartphones are small, general-purpose client computers served by a wireless Wide Area Network. The line is fuzzy: featherweight devices like the Microsoft Surface, MacBook Air and Chromebook blur the line between tablet and laptop.

Mobile devices are a special security concern. Due to their small size they are more frequently lost or stolen than larger devices. Their inherent, and often automated, wireless connectivity makes them more prone to compromise. Integrated radios (cellular network, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC and GPS) provide multiple avenues for security and privacy compromise. And many smartphone applications do not undergo rigorous testing and certification for security flaws.

An organization may require specialized interactive training, such as the Using Mobile Devices in a DoD Environment course on the DoD Cyber Exchange website. It may restrict cellular phone usage, including requiring government-issued devices while on duty, or banning possession of any mobile devices at the workplace. You are responsible for knowing and adhering to the mobile device policy at your unit of assignment.
2.analogy: A mobile device is like a wallet with radios built in: easy to carry everywhere, so it is easy to lose, and its radios are always reaching out, so others have more ways to reach in.
2.scenario: An airman reports to a new unit with a smartphone. It is small, so it is easily lost or stolen, and it connects on its own by Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular, so it is more prone to compromise. The unit requires government-issued devices on duty, so she learns and follows the unit's mobile device policy.
2.example: A paperback book, a pocket radio and a wristwatch are all carried in the hand or on the body, unlike a desktop set. In the course: a mobile device is a client that can be held in the hand, employs a mobile OS, uses a touchscreen as the primary user interface, and uses a wireless network connection, Study Guide p.57.

2.summary: iOS is a UNIX-like operating system for Apple's iPhone and iPod Touch, first released in 2007 with the first-generation iPhone; its user interface is based on direct manipulation such as touch, tap, swipe and pinch.
2.deeper:
iOS is UNIX-like and based on the Darwin XNU kernel. Its code is closed source with some open-source components. Its user interface is based on direct manipulation such as touch, tap, swipe, pinch, reverse pinch, shaking and rotation. It is the second most popular mobile device OS in the world after Android, with about 1.4 billion phones worldwide in 2022. iPadOS is based on iOS but optimized for the Apple iPad, and iOS is also the basis for watchOS and tvOS.

Walled garden model: iPhone applications are available only through the Apple App Store, because Apple restricts third-party app stores and user-directed app installations. This business model is sometimes called a "walled garden". Apple claims this curated approach increases both the quality and security of iPhone applications. In 2022 the App Store held about 2 million apps. Android, based on the Linux kernel and open source, allows sideloading instead.
2.analogy: iOS is like a gated community with one shop inside the gate: residents get everything from that shop, and outside sellers are not let in. Android is a town where anyone can open a stall.
2.scenario: An airman pinches and swipes directly on an iPhone screen; that direct manipulation is the iOS user interface. When she looks for an app from a third-party store, she finds she cannot install it: iPhone apps come only from the Apple App Store.

2.summary: Android was first developed in 2003 by Android, Inc. as an OS for digital cameras and was soon adapted to smart phones; Google bought Android, Inc. in 2005 and released version 1.0 in 2008.
2.deeper:
Android is a UNIX-like, open-source mobile device OS based on the Linux kernel, marketed and maintained by Google LLC. Its source code may be freely copied and distributed, but the term "Android" is trademarked by Google and must be licensed by vendors who wish to use the trademark.

Android, Inc. developed it in 2003, originally as an OS for digital cameras, and it was soon adapted to the rapidly growing smart phone market. Google purchased Android, Inc. in 2005 and released Android OS version 1.0 in 2008. Twenty-one iterations had been released for smart phones by 2022, the latest being Android version 13.

Today it also runs laptop and tablet computers, book readers, game consoles, smart TVs, smart watches, smart boards, media players, home entertainment and home automation systems, and automobiles. Direct manipulation of a touch screen is its primary user interface. In 2022 it ran about 72% of all mobile phones worldwide, and it is the most popular and most widely deployed OS in the world.
2.analogy: Android's path is like a product a small shop first made for one small market: it was soon adapted to a much bigger market, and a large company bought the shop and put its own name behind it.
2.scenario: An airman sees the same OS on a smartphone, a smart TV and a car dashboard. Tracing it back, she finds it began in 2003 as an OS for digital cameras, made by Android, Inc., and was soon adapted to smart phones; Google bought that company in 2005 and released version 1.0 in 2008.
2.example: A tool built for one small job can later be adapted to a much bigger one. In the course: Android was originally designed as an OS for digital cameras but was soon adapted to the rapidly growing smart phone market, Study Guide p.58.

2.summary: Microsoft Office is a family of client software and services developed by Microsoft for Windows and MacOS computers, first released in 1988 as a bundle of Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

Client software includes applications which do real work for users. The first Office release in 1988 bundled the Word word processor, the Excel spreadsheet and the PowerPoint graphical presentation application. The number of bundled apps has since expanded: OneNote (note taking), Publisher (desktop publishing), Access (database), Skype for Business (real-time conferences and meetings), Project (project management) and Teams (a workplace platform for chat, meetings, notes and attachments). Since 2013 Office 365, a cloud-based subscription service, has been Microsoft's preferred mode of delivery.

Microsoft Outlook: the Office app that is a personal manager, calendar, address book and email client. Chat and meetings belong to Teams; Outlook keeps the calendar, the contacts and the email.

Microsoft Visio: the diagram and flowchart creator application. It is not PowerPoint, the graphical presentation program, and not Publisher, the desktop publishing application.

2.summary: Edge is a web browser by Microsoft designed to replace Internet Explorer; it comes bundled with Windows and is a familiar application on the Standard Desktop Configuration.
2.deeper:
Edge is also available for Xbox One, MacOS, iOS and Android. Microsoft describes it as a total reboot and a major improvement over Internet Explorer, with many advanced tools and features such as full integration with the Cortana personal assistant and support for ink on touchscreen computers. In 2018 Microsoft announced that starting in 2020 Edge would be based on the Chromium open-source browser.

Internet Explorer (IE or MSIE) was first released for Windows 95. In 2003 it was the most widely used web browser in the world, with a market share of 95%, but its share has fallen to less than 2%. It remains a legacy application bundled with Windows 10, no longer maintained by Microsoft: on 15 June 2022 Microsoft officially ended support for MSIE. A few legacy applications still require it, so Edge still features an MSIE compatibility mode for legacy applications and web pages which require Internet Explorer.

2.summary: Chromium is a free and open-source browser project supported by Google; Chrome is built on top of it, and at least 20 browsers, including Microsoft Edge, are based on it.
2.deeper:
Chrome is a web browser from Google released on a freeware license. It is supported by many platforms, including Windows, MacOS, Android, iOS and Linux, and it is by far the most popular browser in the world.

Chrome is built on top of the Chromium browser. Using Chromium as a foundation, Google adds a more polished GUI, support for Flash Media, popular video and audio codecs, and comprehensive update support to create Chrome. Because Chromium is free and open-source, at least 20 different web browsers are based on it, including Microsoft Edge: in 2018 Microsoft announced that starting in 2020 Edge would be based on the Chromium open-source browser. The Chrome browser is authorized for use on the Standard Desktop Configuration.

3.summary: The United States Government Configuration Baseline (USGCB) is the standard set of Windows settings that replaced the Federal Desktop Core Configuration (FDCC) for Windows 7.
3.deeper:
The FDCC is a list of standardized Microsoft Windows settings, applications and services recommended by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to create a more secure Windows operating system. Effective February 1, 2008, these mandatory standards applied to every general-purpose desktop or laptop connected to Federal Government office networks. The FDCC applied only to Windows XP and Vista; the USGCB replaced it for Windows 7.

In 2016 the USAF began a service-wide effort to upgrade to Windows 10 via the SDC. Installed as a disk image, the SDC gives a single standard, enterprise-wide managed environment across the Air Force Network. It is a necessary compromise between security and usability: normal users have no administrator privileges and the software store is very limited, because administrator privileges for all users would be an untenable security situation. The SDC still gives centralized control over applications, updates and security patches (access control) while providing useful workstations.
3.analogy: A standard baseline is like one uniform standard for a whole unit: when a new standard comes in, it replaces the old one, and everyone follows the same one.
3.scenario: An airman traces the standard Windows settings used on government office networks. Windows XP and Vista computers followed the FDCC. Windows 7 computers followed the USGCB, which replaced it. Windows 10 computers on the Air Force Network get the SDC, installed as a disk image. Each one kept every computer on one standard configuration.
3.example: A school that gives every classroom the same approved computer setup, instead of letting each teacher choose, keeps every room alike. 3.summary: An update policy is the rule set an administrator establishes, applied to all user accounts, to keep the operating system up to date with the latest security patches.
3.deeper: Because the threat landscape is constantly evolving, operating systems must be kept up to date with the latest security patches. Establishing an update policy that applies to all user accounts is a core administrator duty. An operating system that is missing security patches is a network vulnerability. If a client falls too far behind on security updates, it may be denied access to the network until it can be re-imaged. Update policy is one part of basic security configuration, with password policy, access control, antivirus programs and firewalls.
3.analogy: An update policy is like a shot schedule for a whole unit: everyone gets the new shots on time, and someone far behind may be kept out of shared spaces until caught up.
3.scenario: An airman finds a client that has missed months of security patches. Its operating system is now a network vulnerability, and because it has fallen too far behind, it is denied access to the network until it is re-imaged. An update policy applied to all user accounts would have kept it current.
3.example: A phone that keeps installing its security updates stays protected as new problems appear. In the course: due to the constantly evolving threat landscape operating systems must be kept up to date with the latest security patches, Study Guide p.64.

3.summary: A Windows Administrator account gives full control over the system and over all other user accounts; the administrator decides what each other user can and can't do with the PC.
3.deeper:
Windows 10 controls access by providing different account types secured with passwords. The administrator controls the entire computer, including who gets to use it and what each user may do with it; on a computer running Windows, the owner usually holds the Administrator account. The administrator sets up an account for each additional user and can limit their access with folder and file encryption or folder and file permissions, so a user account has limited privileges assigned by the administrator. A Standard account can access most of the computer but can't change other accounts and has no access to the administrator's files or folders. A Child account is a Standard account with the Family Safety settings automatically turned on. A Guest account works much like a Standard account, with no privacy.

Kiosk mode: a kiosk is a special account that requires no logon credentials. The kiosk user doesn't need to sign on and can use only one application, such as a web browser, a game or a sign-in page, and can't make any changes to the system.
3.analogy: The administrator is like a building owner who hands out keys: one key opens most rooms, a visitor's key opens the lobby, and one key opens only the mailbox. The owner decides who gets which key.
3.scenario: An airman sets up a lobby computer that must run only a sign-in page, with no logon and no changes to the system. Using the Administrator account, the airman makes it a kiosk, and keeps control over every other account on the PC.
3.example: A building manager holds the master key and decides which rooms each tenant may open. In the course: an Administrator account gives the Administrator full control over the system as well as control over all other user accounts, Study Guide p.64.

3.summary: A Windows Guest account lets someone use the computer without being recognized by name; it works much like a Standard account but with no privacy.
3.deeper: Anybody can sign in with the Guest account, and the desktop looks the way the last guest left it. Guest users can't add or remove software or make any system changes, so the account is great for web browsing or checking email but not much else. 3.analogy: A Guest account is like a shared computer in a library: anyone can sit down, nobody is asked their name, and the screen is just as the last person left it.
3.scenario: A visitor needs to check email on an office PC. The airman points the visitor to the Guest account: the visitor can browse and read mail, the computer does not know who is signed in, and nothing can be installed or changed. The next guest will find the desktop the way this one left it.

3.summary: A Windows 10 Local account doesn't require users to log on to a Microsoft account, or even a network connection; it is the most PC-centric way to set up Windows 10.
3.deeper:
A Local account enhances privacy and security, but it deprives the Windows user of the many services available through a Microsoft account. Administrator, Standard User, Guest and Kiosk accounts may still be created on a Local account. Microsoft services are disabled or limited: without a Microsoft account, free apps are still available in the Windows App Store but paid apps are not, settings are not backed up to an account to restore across devices, and Cortana works only in a limited capacity. A Microsoft account also gives free Hotmail or Outlook email and is needed for Xbox.

OneDrive: OneDrive is the Microsoft cloud storage service. With a Microsoft account you get 5GB of free space, and more by paying a fee; it is one of the services a Local account goes without.
3.analogy: A Local account is like a notebook kept in your own desk instead of a shared online folder: nobody else's system is involved, but you also give up the backups and extras the online folder offers.
3.scenario: An airman sets up Windows 10 on a computer with no network connection, so a Microsoft account is not an option and the airman creates a Local account. 3.summary: A virus definition is a binary pattern, like a digital fingerprint, that identifies a specific virus; basic antivirus programs compare files to a list of these definitions.
3.deeper:
Antivirus software is a program designed to protect computers from malware such as viruses, computer worms, spyware, botnets, rootkits and keyloggers; antivirus programs scan, detect and remove viruses. Basic antivirus programs work by comparing a program or file on the computer to a list of virus definitions contained in a database. Almost all antivirus programs feature automatic updates: both the software and the virus definitions in its database are regularly updated to stay ahead of new or evolving threats, because bad actors keep creating new viruses and malware. Basic antivirus is highly effective against known viruses, but less so against new viruses that have not yet been added to the database.

Antivirus quarantine: if a file matches a definition, the antivirus program takes additional action to remove or isolate (quarantine) the suspicious file.
3.analogy: Virus definitions work like a wall of wanted posters: a guard compares each face to the posters, and a match is held aside. A face not yet on the wall walks past.
3.scenario: An airman's antivirus program checks a downloaded file. It compares the file to the virus definitions in its database, finds a match, and isolates the file in quarantine. Later, its automatic updates add new definitions so it can recognize newer viruses.
3.example: A fingerprint on file lets an investigator say exactly whose print was found. In the course: a virus definition is a binary pattern, like a digital fingerprint, which identifies a specific virus, Study Guide p.65.

3.summary: Heuristics analysis is a more advanced kind of antivirus that detects malware by its behavior, scanning for suspicious or malicious computer activity instead of known virus signatures.
3.deeper:
Basic antivirus programs compare files to a database of virus definitions, so they are highly effective against known viruses but less so against new viruses that have not yet been added to the database. Heuristics analysis uses heuristics, or behavior, instead: if something acts like malware, it probably is. Antivirus programs are not perfect and may not detect every infection, so an antivirus program is not a stand-alone defense for a client device; it is part of a multilayered strategy that includes access control and one or more firewalls.

Zero-day malware: new or unknown malware, not yet in the virus definitions database, is zero-day malware. Heuristics analysis is more effective against it, because it scans for suspicious or malicious activity rather than specific known viruses.
3.analogy: Basic antivirus is a guard with a list of known faces; heuristics is a guard who watches what people do. A stranger who is on no list can still be stopped for acting suspiciously.
3.scenario: A new piece of malware reaches a client before any virus definition exists for it, so a basic signature check finds no match. A program using heuristics analysis notices the program acting in a suspicious, malicious way and flags it: if something acts like malware, it probably is.
3.example: A store detective who watches for someone slipping items into a coat can catch a first-time shoplifter that no photo would match. In the course: heuristics analysis is more effective against new or unknown (zero-day) malware because it scans for suspicious or malicious computer activity rather than specific known viruses, Study Guide p.66.

3.summary: Microsoft Defender is the free antivirus program built into Windows 10; it offers automatic, real-time protection and manual scanning against a wide range of malware.
3.deeper: Most antivirus programs have both manual and automatic scanning. Automatic scanning gives instant, real-time reaction to dangerous downloads, portable media that has just been mounted to the computer, and files created by software installers. Manual scanning lets an alert user scan a specific suspicious folder, or even a single file, to see whether it is harmful before opening or executing it. Microsoft Defender offers both. It integrates with the Microsoft Internet Explorer and Microsoft Edge web browsers to scan files as they are being downloaded, and integration with the Google Chrome browser is available through a browser extension. Like any antivirus program, it may not detect every infection, so it is not a stand-alone defense: it is one layer of a strategy that includes access control and one or more firewalls.
3.analogy: Microsoft Defender's two modes are like a smoke detector and a flashlight: the detector reacts on its own the moment smoke appears, and the flashlight lets you check one dark corner yourself before you step in.
3.scenario: An airman plugs in a USB drive, and Microsoft Defender's automatic, real-time scanning reacts at once. Later the airman doubts one file and runs a manual scan of just that file before opening it. Access control and the firewall stay in place too, because antivirus alone is not enough.
3.example: A building with a guard at the door and a check-in desk inside does not rely on one of them alone. In the course: Windows 10 includes a free, built-in antivirus program called Microsoft Defender which offers automatic, real-time protection as well as manual scanning capability, Study Guide p.66.

3.summary: A software firewall is a program installed on each computer that monitors ports and applications and blocks any connection that violates the rule set.
3.deeper:
A firewall is a security device that monitors both incoming and outgoing network traffic and permits or blocks data packets based on a predefined set of rules; along with access control and antivirus programs, firewalls give an additional measure to secure client devices. The two main types of firewalls are hardware and software. Windows 10 includes a free, built-in firewall that is preconfigured and turned on by default. Firewall configuration is an important administrator function: casual users get a simple menu of basic, preconfigured (recommended) settings, and skilled administrators get an advanced settings menu.

Hardware firewall: a hardware firewall is installed on a piece of physical equipment, such as a network gateway, located between the computer and the network. The hardware firewall on a residential router protects every device connected to it by acting as an intermediary between the local area network and the public Internet, while a software firewall protects the computer it is installed on.
3.analogy: A hardware firewall is the gate to a whole neighborhood; a software firewall is the lock on each house's own door.
3.scenario: At home, an airman's residential router has a hardware firewall that stands between the local area network and the public Internet for every connected device. The airman's Windows 10 laptop also runs its built-in software firewall, turned on by default, which watches that laptop's own ports and applications and blocks any connection that breaks its rules.
3.example: Each apartment has its own door lock, even in a building with a locked front entrance. In the course: a software firewall is a program installed on each computer which monitors ports and applications and blocks any connection which violates the rule set, Study Guide p.66.

4.summary: Software piracy is the unauthorized copying or distribution of copyrighted software, by copying, downloading, sharing, selling or installing it on personal or work computers.
4.deeper:
When you purchase software, you are purchasing a license to use it, not the actual software, and the license tells you how many times you can install it. The EULA (End User License Agreement) tells you how many copies you may use and how long you may use them; it is legally binding, like a contract. Making more copies than the license permits is piracy, and any use beyond the scope of the license is a violation of it and possibly an act of piracy. Deliberate or not, software piracy is illegal and punishable by law. It comes in many forms, including corporate or end-user piracy, Internet piracy, subscription licensing piracy and counterfeiting.

Subscription licensing piracy: using subscription licensed software past the subscription date.

Software counterfeiting: someone copies the product and its packaging so that it looks like an original.
4.analogy: Buying software is like buying a concert ticket: you pay for the right to attend, not for the band. Using one ticket to let five friends in breaks its terms, whether you meant to or not.
4.scenario: An airman buys one license for a program and installs it on three computers, thinking that is fine. The license permits one installation, so the extra copies go beyond its scope: this is software piracy, and it is illegal even though it was not deliberate.
4.example: Photocopying a whole textbook instead of buying copies gives away what the author sells. In the course: software piracy is the unauthorized copying or distribution of copyrighted software, Study Guide p.68.

4.summary: Authorized purposes are brief personal communications that DoD employees may make on federal government communications systems, such as telling family of official transportation or schedule changes.
4.deeper:
DoD 5500.07-R, the Joint Ethics Regulation, gives guidance for the ethical use of Air Force computer systems and networks: communications systems provided by the federal government, including email, internet systems and commercial systems, are for official use and authorized purposes only. Authorized purposes include brief communications by DoD employees traveling on government business to notify family members of official transportation or schedule changes. They also include personal communications from the usual workplace that are most reasonably made there, such as checking in with a spouse or minor children, scheduling doctor and auto or home repair appointments, brief internet searches, and emailing directions to visiting relatives. The employee's agency must determine that such communications do not adversely affect official duties, are of reasonable duration and frequency, serve a legitimate public interest, and do not reflect adversely on the DoD, for example through pornography, chain letters, unofficial advertising, soliciting or selling, violations of regulation, or classified information.

Official use: official use includes emergency communications and communications the DoD Component determines are necessary in the interest of the Federal Government. When theater commanders approve it in the interest of morale and welfare, it may include communications by military members and other DoD employees deployed for extended periods away from home on official DoD business.
4.analogy: A work phone is like a company truck: you drive it for the job, and a short, reasonable stop on the way is allowed, but not a weekend road trip.
4.scenario: An airman traveling on government business learns the flight home is delayed and sends a brief message to family about the schedule change. Later, at the usual workplace, the airman schedules a doctor appointment. Both are authorized purposes, as long as they are brief and do not get in the way of official duties.
4.example: An employer that lets workers make a quick call home from the office phone still expects the phone to be used mainly for work. In the course: authorized purposes include brief communications made by DoD employees while they are traveling on Government business to notify family members of official transportation or schedule changes, Study Guide p.71.

4.summary: The host or tenant Accountable Property Officer (APO) appoints the Base Software License Managers (BSLMs) and certifies their annual software inventory; software license management on an installation is centralized, but no lower than the APO.
4.deeper: According to DAFMAN 17-1203, ultimate responsibility for software piracy prevention lies with the Chief Information Officer (SAF/CN). The host or tenant APO appoints primary and alternate BSLMs to manage the wing and base software license programs, including tenant units. The APO certifies that the BSLM has conducted an annual inventory of all software on an installation and provides a copy of the inventory to their MAJCOM A/6 or Field Command (FLDCOM) and the Service Owner for Enterprise IT. The BSLM is responsible for practical implementation of Air Force software control and anti-piracy policy and prevents piracy primarily through careful management of software licenses: it ensures inventories are kept and conducted, monitors automated inventories, provides license training and performs compliance visits. Individual Air Force organizations keep a software license inventory and proof of license ownership, store license proof securely, inventory all licensed software annually, and audit all systems for illegal or unauthorized copies; the organization commander certifies the annual inventory and submits it to the BSLM.
4.analogy: The APO is like a supply officer who names the clerks who keep the stock list, and at the end of the year signs that the count was done before sending it up the chain.
4.scenario: At a base, the APO appoints a primary and an alternate BSLM. Each organization inventories its licensed software for the year, and its commander certifies the inventory and submits it to the BSLM. The APO then certifies that the BSLM conducted the annual inventory and sends a copy to the MAJCOM A/6 or FLDCOM and the Service Owner for Enterprise IT.

4.summary: Classified information transmission means sending classified information only with approved security procedures and practices, such as encryption, secure networks and secure workstations.
4.deeper: Most federal government communications are not secure. DoD employees shall not transmit classified information over any communication system unless it is transmitted using approved security procedures and practices, for example encryption, secure networks and secure workstations. In addition, DoD employees shall not release access information, such as passwords, to anyone unless specifically authorized to do so. Use of government systems is also not anonymous: under DoD Instruction 8560.01, using them serves as consent to monitoring of any type of use, and the name and computer address of the user are recorded for each use of the internet.
4.analogy: Sending classified information is like moving cash between banks: you don't mail it in a plain envelope, you use the armored truck the rules require.
4.scenario: An airman needs to send classified information to another office. Ordinary government email is not secure, so the airman uses an approved practice: encryption over a secure network from a secure workstation. When a coworker asks for the airman's password to help, the airman refuses, because releasing access information needs specific authorization.
4.example: A bank moves money between branches in an armored truck, not by regular mail. 4.deeper: A successful civil lawsuit by the owner of a software copyright normally requires the violator to pay for all monetary losses to the copyright owner and to turn over any profits the violator earned from misuse of the copyrighted software. A civil court judge may also impose a fine of up to $150,000 per violation. If the act of software piracy is judged to be a criminal act akin to stealing, the violator could be charged with a criminal offense and, if found guilty, sentenced to up to 5 years in jail and required to pay a fine of up to $250,000. Software piracy is illegal and punishable by law whether it is deliberate or not.
4.analogy: It is like taking a neighbor's car without asking: the owner can sue you to pay for the harm, and if it was theft, you can also be prosecuted.
4.scenario: A company that copied software without licenses is sued by the copyright owner. The civil court orders it to pay the owner's monetary losses, turn over the profits it earned from the misuse, and pay a fine per violation. Had the act been judged criminal, akin to stealing, jail time would also have been possible.
4.example: Copying a hit song and selling it can bring a lawsuit from the songwriter. In the course: US law provides both civil and criminal penalties for software piracy which is considered a form of copyright infringement, Study Guide p.70.

5.summary: A clean install, also known as a bare metal install, is a deployment where the administrator installs Windows on a single PC from DVD or USB media.
5.deeper:
Several deployment models are available for installing Windows OS in enterprise networks. A clean install is the most time- and labor-intensive method. It must be done on-premises for each individual PC, so it is impractical if the network contains more than a few computers. A disk clone, by contrast, copies one hard disk drive onto another, OS, settings, saved files and applications included. A clean install needs preparation: access to a working PC with at least one storage drive, a portable or network drive for file backup if required, access to the BIOS CMOS settings, Windows installation media, a Windows activation key, and an optional Internet connection for important updates and Microsoft account services. The activation key can come supplied with the purchased media, be already associated with or printed on the computer, come from digital entitlement, or be bought new from a commercial vendor.

Digital entitlement: a valid activation key is already associated with the PC because of an older Windows installation, such as Windows 7. If the licensee is entitled to a free upgrade to a newer Windows version, this activation key can be reused.
5.analogy: A clean install is like building a house from the ground up on an empty lot: thorough, but nobody would build a whole neighborhood one house at a time this way.
5.scenario: An airman must put Windows on one PC with a brand-new drive. The airman gathers the installation media on a USB flash drive and an activation key, and installs Windows on that single PC on site. For a whole network of computers, the airman would pick another deployment model.
5.example: Writing each invitation by hand works for a few guests, but not for hundreds. In the course: since it must be accomplished on-premises for each individual PC, clean install is impractical if the network contains more than a few computers, Study Guide p.73.

5.summary: A disk clone is a deployment method in which the administrator uses disk cloning software to make an exact copy of one hard disk drive onto another, which can then be installed in another computer.
5.deeper: Disk cloning copies not only the OS but also configuration settings, desktop layout, all saved files and all applications installed on the parent disk. This is useful for deploying a standard configuration across several identical PC workstations, and it is a good option for an individual who wants to upgrade to a new HDD without losing any files, applications or configuration settings. Disk cloning allows unattended installation, but it can be time-consuming. Cloning works best when the parent PC and the destination PC are the same make and model with identical hardware. Windows and every licensed application on the cloned disk need software licenses for each additional PC: software licenses can't be cloned.
5.analogy: A disk clone is like photocopying a filled-in form instead of starting a blank one: every answer comes along, but each copy still needs its own signature, the license.
5.scenario: An airman's workstation needs a new HDD. The airman clones the old drive onto the new one, so the OS, settings, saved files and applications all come along. When the same disk image goes to three more identical PCs, each of them needs its own software licenses.
5.example: Copying an entire phone onto a new phone of the same model keeps every app and setting in place. In the course: disk cloning has the advantage of copying not only the OS, but also configuration settings, desktop layout, all saved files, and all applications installed on the parent disk, Study Guide p.74.

5.summary: The Pre-boot Execution Environment (PXE, also called "pixie") is a BIOS service that lets modern motherboards boot over a local area network (LAN).
5.deeper:
With network boot, Windows loads from a remote server instead of being installed locally on the user's PC, which gives the administrator full control over user settings, security updates, patches and user applications. Network boot can also be used to install Windows on a client PC: a preconfigured Windows disk image is downloaded from a remote server and installed on the client's boot drive.

Unattended installation: this kind of install is typically assisted by an automatic prompt script. A small program answers all the yes and no prompts that pop up during an install, so the administrator doesn't have to sit with the machine and respond to every prompt. Disk cloning also allows unattended installation.
5.analogy: PXE is like a new arrival who shows up with empty hands and is given a ready kit at the front desk; the prompt script is a helper who fills in every form for them.
5.scenario: An airman needs Windows on a client PC without carrying media to it. The motherboard boots over the LAN using PXE, downloads a preconfigured Windows disk image from a remote server, and installs it on the boot drive while an automatic prompt script answers every yes and no prompt.
5.example: Streaming a show from a server, instead of buying the disc, means nothing has to be stored at home first. In the course: modern motherboards support booting over a local area network (LAN) using a BIOS service called Pre-boot Execution Environment (PXE), Study Guide p.74.

5.summary: Windows Autopilot is a paid Microsoft subscription service that re-images clients remotely over a network connection, so a new PC can go straight to the end user.
5.deeper: New computers bought in bulk usually come with a licensed OEM version of Windows preinstalled. Re-imaging them to the corporate standard and adding them to the corporate network can be very time- and labor-intensive, with extensive hands-on activity by IT staff. Autopilot solves this by allowing remote re-imaging of clients over a network connection. It needs vendor involvement: the new machines must be preregistered with Microsoft so that Autopilot can automatically discover and provision them the first time they connect to a network. The new PC can then be delivered directly to the end user with no need for IT staff involvement: the employee unboxes it, plugs it in and turns it on, and a remote Autopilot server does the rest.
5.analogy: Autopilot is like a delivery that sets itself up: the box arrives at your desk, you plug it in, and it arranges itself to the company standard without a technician.
5.scenario: An organization buys new PCs in bulk. The vendor preregisters them with Microsoft and ships one straight to an airman's desk. The airman unboxes it, plugs it in and turns it on; on its first network connection, a remote Autopilot server discovers it and provisions it.
5.example: A new appliance that registers itself and downloads its settings when first plugged in needs no technician visit. In the course: Windows Autopilot solves this problem by allowing remote re-imaging of clients over a network connection, Study Guide p.74.
